cards.title: P versus NP
cards.formal: Does every language with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates admit a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,k such that, for every encoded Boolean formula F of bit length n, A decides whether F has a satisfying assignment and halts within $C(n+1)^k$ steps? The algorithm must give the correct answer on every input.
cards.definitions: A language is a subset of the finite binary strings. P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with worst-case running time \(C(n+1)^{k}\) for some constants C,k. NP consists of languages L for which there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p satisfying $x\in L\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1$. The verifier's time is polynomial in the combined input length. SAT is the language of well-formed Boolean formulas with at least one satisfying assignment; malformed encodings are rejected. Fix any ordinary explicit binary encoding of formulas using AND, OR, and NOT. The question concerns uniform deterministic computation, with no advice, oracle, or error probability. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) or \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the deterministic uniform model defined here. Equality requires that every NP language have a polynomial-time decision algorithm; inequality requires that at least one NP language have none.
cards.status_note: The Clay Mathematics Institute lists P versus NP as unsolved, checked on 11 September 2026. The cited restricted-circuit lower bounds and proof-method barriers do not resolve the uniform decision problem.

cards.title: P versus PSPACE
cards.formal: Does every language decidable by a deterministic Turing machine using polynomial working space have a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a machine A and constants C,k such that A decides truth of every closed quantified Boolean formula of encoded length n in at most $C(n+1)^k$ steps?
cards.definitions: P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed polynomial worst-case time bound. PSPACE consists of languages decided by one deterministic Turing machine which halts on every input and visits at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) work-tape cells, for some constants C,k, on inputs of length n. The input is read-only and is not charged as work space; a fixed finite tape alphabet is used. PSPACE imposes no polynomial time bound. A closed quantified Boolean formula has the form \(Q_{1}x_{1}\cdots Q_{m}x_{m} \varphi (x_{1},\ldots ,x_{m})\), where each \(Q_{i}\) is \(\exists\) or \(\forall\), quantified variables are distinct, and \(\varphi\) is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula using AND, OR, and NOT, with no free variables. Every quantifier ranges over \(\{0,1\}\). The number of quantifiers and their alternations may grow with n; the input is not restricted to a fixed number of blocks. Use any standard explicit binary encoding, reject malformed inputs, and count its full bit length n. Truth means the usual nested Boolean quantifier semantics. This language, TQBF, is PSPACE-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions. No oracle, advice, randomization, or promise is allowed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\) or \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{PSPACE}\). The first outcome asserts a deterministic polynomial-time decision procedure for every polynomial-space language; the second asserts a polynomial-space language with no deterministic polynomial-time decision procedure.
cards.status_note: Primary-source review and a search for subsequent results on 11 September 2026 found no resolution. Williams’ 2025 simulation and August 2026 MFCS survey concern time-space bounds; neither states an equality or separation of P and PSPACE.

cards.title: L versus P
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{P}\)? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have a deterministic algorithm that always halts and uses \(O(\log (n+2))\) bits of working memory on an input of binary encoding length n?
cards.definitions: L consists of total decision languages recognized by a fixed deterministic Turing machine with a read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank read/write work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. The input can be revisited freely; all visited work-tape cells count toward space, but the read-only input itself does not. For each language there must be a constant C such that every n-bit input uses at most \(C \log _{2}(n+2)\) work bits and the machine halts. Acceptance is a final state, not a long output tape usable as memory. A halting machine in this model has only polynomially many possible configurations on a fixed input, so its time is automatically polynomial. P is the class of languages decided by uniform deterministic Turing machines in \(O((n+2)^{c})\) time for some fixed c. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered DAG of AND, OR, and NOT gates, Boolean input values, and one designated output gate, and asks whether its value is 1. The entire gate and input encoding counts toward n; malformed encodings are rejected. There are no random bits, oracle, advice, auxiliary catalytic tape, or restrictions on circuit depth. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{P}\) or \(\mathrm{L}\ne \mathrm{P}\) in the read-only-input model defined here. Equality means that every polynomial-time decision language admits a halting deterministic logarithmic-space machine; inequality means that at least one such language admits none.
cards.status_note: The Winter 2026 logarithmic-space notes explicitly leave the basic containments unresolved. A primary-source and later-result search on 11 September 2026 found no resolution of L versus P. The square-root-space simulation remains above logarithmic space for general polynomial-time computations.

cards.title: Nonuniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) versus \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\)
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\subsetneq \mathrm{NC}^{1}\) for the nonuniform circuit classes defined below? Equivalently, does there exist a Boolean function family \(f=(f_{n}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\})\) in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) such that for every fixed depth \(d\ge 1\), exponent \(k\ge 1\), and constant \(M\ge 1\), there is an n for which every depth-at-most-d majority circuit computing \(f_{n}\) exactly has size greater than \(M(n+1)^{k}\)?
cards.definitions: A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\), optional constants 0,1, and one output. Depth is the maximum number of gates on an input-to-output path. Size is the number of gates plus the number of wires; if an input is repeated at a gate, each occurrence counts as a wire. A majority circuit has AND and OR gates of arbitrary positive fan-in, NOT gates of fan-in one, and MAJ gates of arbitrary positive fan-in m, with output 1 exactly when strictly more than \(m/2\) inputs equal 1. \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) consists of all families with such circuits of size \(M(n+1)^{k}\) and depth at most d for every n, for some constants M,k,d depending on the family. \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) consists of families with circuits over AND, OR, NOT, with fan-in at most two (one for NOT), size \(M(n+1)^{k}\), and depth at most \(b \log _{2}(n+1)\), for fixed M,k,b. Circuits may share intermediate gates. Both classes are nonuniform: an arbitrary separate circuit may be chosen for each input length, without any requirement to compute its description. The output must be correct on every input; no randomness, approximation, promise, or distributional error is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\subsetneq \mathrm{NC}^{1}\) or \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}=\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) for the nonuniform families defined here. Strictness requires a single \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) family with no polynomial-size constant-depth majority-circuit family; equality requires that every \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) family admit such a family.
cards.status_note: The source and subsequent-work checks on 11 September 2026 found no equality or separation of these nonuniform classes. The 2026 depth-two result concerns a function in \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\) and polynomial circuit size; the typed-monoid result concerns uniform classes. These conclusions have different quantifiers and models from the target.

cards.title: Berman–Hartmanis conjecture
cards.formal: For every pair of languages \(A,B\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* that are NP-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, does there exist a bijection \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* such that f and \(f^{- 1}\) are computable in deterministic polynomial time and, for every string \(x, x\in A\) if and only if \(f(x)\in B\)?
cards.definitions: A language is a set of finite binary strings, including a specified membership decision for every string; malformed encodings are therefore part of the language convention. NP consists of languages L for which \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) exactly when some witness of length polynomial in |x| is accepted by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. A many-one reduction from L to A is a total deterministic polynomial-time function g with \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) iff \(g(x)\in A\). A is NP-complete if \(A\in \mathrm{NP}\) and every \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{NP}\) reduces to A in this sense. The desired f is a permutation of all finite binary strings, taking members to members and nonmembers to nonmembers. Its running time is polynomial in its input length, and its inverse has a polynomial bound in the inverse input length. The algorithms and polynomial bounds may depend on the fixed pair A,B, but not on the particular input string. No advice, oracle, randomness or length-preservation requirement is allowed. This is the unconditional conjecture; \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) is not an assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every pair of polynomial-time many-one NP-complete languages is polynomial-time isomorphic, or prove that some pair has no bijection with both directions computable in polynomial time. The statement is unconditional: \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) is not an added hypothesis.
cards.status_note: The 2022 primary-author problem column states that the full conjecture is open. A later-source search on 11 September 2026 located the 2025 recovery-reduction preprint, which still uses it as a conjectural hypothesis, and found no resolution. Its truth-table recovery consequence is conditional.

cards.title: Expected linear-time integer sorting for every word length
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform Las Vegas word-RAM algorithm and a constant \(C\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), every integer word length \(w\ge\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\), and every list \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\), the algorithm outputs the list in nondecreasing order with expected running time at most \(Cn\)?
cards.definitions: The input occupies n words, with one unsigned w-bit key per word; repeated keys are allowed. The output must contain exactly the input multiset in nondecreasing numerical order, with no stability requirement. The machine is sequential and has w-bit data registers and random-access memory. Unit-cost operations are reads and writes, comparisons, branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication of two words with the product returned in two words, quotient and remainder of two words with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and left or right shifts by a word-specified amount. Shifted-out bits are discarded, and shifts by at least w return zero. Addresses may use a constant number of words to index polynomially many memory cells; all address computation is charged. An operation can generate one fresh independent uniform w-bit random word. These are the only primitive operations; arbitrary-length arithmetic, a built-in sorting operation and free tables are unavailable. All preprocessing, memory initialization performed by the algorithm, and output writes count. A fixed finite program receives n and w; it may select methods according to their values but has no advice depending on them. Las Vegas means every terminating computation is correct and the algorithm terminates with probability one. Expectation is over the internal random choices for each fixed input. C must be independent of both n and w, including when w grows with n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a single uniform, always-correct Las Vegas program whose expected running time is at most Cn on every admissible (n,w,input), for one C independent of n and w. A negative answer must show that every such sorting program has unbounded expected-time/n ratio over these inputs. A lower bound only for comparison sorting, deterministic programs, or a different word instruction set does not establish that negation.
cards.status_note: The checked primary bounds and the CMU Spring 2025 source leave expected linear-time sorting across all word lengths open. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no result settling this full target. Recent parallel sorting results for keys in \([n]\) concern a restricted universe and a different performance model.

cards.title: Sorting \(X + Y\)
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic real-RAM algorithm A and a constant C such that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every \(X=(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}), Y=(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{n})\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}, A\) outputs a permutation \(((i_{1},j_{1}),\ldots ,(i_{n^{2}},j_{n^{2}}))\) of \([n]\times [n]\) satisfying \(x_{i_{r}}+y_{j_{r}}\le x_{i_{r+1}}+y_{j_{r+1}}\) for \(1\le r<n^{2}\), in at most \(Cn^{2}\) unit-cost operations?
cards.definitions: The input consists of n and the 2n exact real numbers in random-access arrays; no sortedness, distinctness, integrality or magnitude bound is promised. All \(n^{2}\) index pairs must occur once in the output, including pairs with equal sums. Ties may appear in any order. A real RAM has exact real registers and cells, supporting copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero reals and comparisons at unit cost. A fixed finite program may use rational constants, with no advice depending on n. It also has integer registers and cells of \(b=d\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for some fixed integer \(d\ge 3\) chosen with the algorithm. Integer instructions are copy, comparison, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b}\), quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts; shifts by at least b return zero. Integer addresses access individual real or integer cells, and each read or write costs one operation. Integer-to-real conversion is permitted, but real-to-integer conversion, floor on reals, extraction of their bits and arbitrary-precision integer operations are not primitives. Memory starts empty apart from the input and fixed program constants; all preprocessing, table construction, address computation and output writes are charged. The algorithm must halt correctly on every input and uses no randomness. Constants C and d are independent of n and of the real values. This is the quadratic-time real-RAM version explicitly asked in the cited necklace paper and identified as the main target in TOPP. Indexed multiset output resolves possible equal sums; allowing repeated input entries does not change the target, since repetitions can be grouped by \(O(n \log  n)\) comparison sorting and expanded within the output budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one uniform deterministic program with a proof of exact output correctness and the \(O(n^{2})\) worst-case total-time bound for every real input, or prove that no such program exists in the specified model. Equivalently, a negative answer shows that every correct program has unbounded worst-case running-time/\(n^{2}\) ratio. Neither a bound only on the number of comparisons nor an algorithm restricted to bounded integers resolves this claim.
cards.status_note: TOPP Problem 41, primary comparison and real-RAM sources, and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No uniform quadratic-time algorithm or matching impossibility result for the stated real-valued problem was found. The \(2017/2018\) decision-tree result does not settle total time. This is a source review, not an independent proof audit.

cards.title: Hypergraph cut sparsifiers with \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) hyperedges
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that every nonnegatively weighted hypergraph \(H\) on \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge2\), and every real \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) admit a nonnegatively weighted hypergraph \(H'\) on the same vertices with \(|E'|\le Cn/\varepsilon^2\) and \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{cut}_H(S)\le\operatorname{cut}_{H'}(S)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{cut}_H(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\)?
cards.definitions: For \(n\ge2\), write \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A weighted hypergraph \(H=(V,E,w)\) has a set \(E\subseteq\{e\subseteq V:|e|\ge2\}\) and finite nonnegative real weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). For every \(S\subseteq V\), set \(\operatorname{cut}_H(S)=\sum_{\substack{e\in E:\ e\cap S\ne\varnothing,\\e\cap(V\setminus S)\ne\varnothing}}w(e)\). Thus each crossing hyperedge contributes its weight exactly once, regardless of the number of vertices on either side. Empty and singleton edges are omitted because they cross no cut; repeated edges can be merged by summing weights. The approximating hypergraph \(H'=(V,E',w')\) follows the same rules. Its edge set may contain any subsets of the original vertex set, not necessarily original edges; additional vertices are forbidden. Size is \(|E'|\), rather than the sum of edge cardinalities or a bit-encoding length. The same approximation must hold for all cuts simultaneously, and a zero-valued original cut must remain exactly zero. The empty edge set is allowed. This is an existence question with no construction-time, randomness or rational-weight restriction. The constant \(C\) is independent of dimension, accuracy, hyperedge count, maximum edge size and weights.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of this universal existence theorem with one constant \(C\), or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every \(C>0\), some permitted \(n,H,\varepsilon\) has no same-vertex weighted hypergraph meeting both the size and all-cut guarantees. A refutation must allow arbitrary nonnegative replacement hyperedges, not just sampled original edges. A size bound retaining an unbounded logarithmic factor does not establish the stated theorem.
cards.status_note: The original source permits arbitrary weighted replacement hyperedges on the same vertex set. The reviewed general upper bound has a logarithmic factor; later sketching and streaming-space results do not themselves remove it. A bounded 13 September 2026 later-work search did not locate a matching existence theorem or refutation. Cited proofs were not independently verified.

cards.title: Near-linear-time approximation of reachability diameter
cards.formal: For an unweighted directed graph $G=(V,E)$, define $D(G)=\max\{d_G(u,v):d_G(u,v)<\infty\}$. Is there an absolute constant $C\ge1$ and one randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every input, returns an estimate $D(G)/C\le\widehat D\le D(G)$ with probability at least \(2/3\) in $\widetilde O(n+m)$ worst-case time? Here $n=|V|$, $m=|E|$, words have $\Theta(\log n)$ bits, and self-distances are included, giving \(D(G)=0\) on an edgeless graph. The constant and the hidden logarithmic exponent are independent of G.
cards.definitions: Distances count edges on a shortest directed path. The maximum concerns finite distances only; it is neither the longest simple path nor the maximum of the smaller of the two directional distances. $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. This card focuses the broader approximation–time tradeoff on near-linear running time.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a randomized algorithm and one absolute constant C meeting the displayed guarantee in near-linear time on every directed graph, or prove that no constant approximation is possible with that time bound.

cards.title: Near-linear output-sensitive Subset Sum
cards.formal: Do there exist a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm and constants \(C>0\), \(b\ge0\) that, given \(n\ge1\) positive integers \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\le t\) and an integer \(t\ge1\), output exactly the distinct values in \(S(X,t)=\{\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}:I\subseteq[n]\}\cap\{0,\ldots,t\}\) in at most \(C(n+|S(X,t)|)(\log(n+t+2))^{b}\) operations?
cards.definitions: The input is an explicitly listed multiset; repeated values are allowed and each index can be selected at most once. The empty subset contributes zero. Output every attainable value once, in any order, with no requirement to list subsets or witnesses. Inputs exceeding the threshold can be discarded when represented in the same word model. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+t+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The word-size constant and all time constants are independent of both \(n\) and \(t\). The target permits polylogarithmic dependence on the numerical threshold, but no linear scan of its universe unless covered by the stated output bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the specified model, quantifiers and guarantees. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean; a partial improvement does not meet the target.

cards.title: Maximum reset threshold of synchronizing automata
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 1\), determine \(T(n)=\max\){\(rt(A): A\) is a synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with n states and any finite nonempty alphabet}, where \(rt(A)\) is its shortest reset-word length.
cards.definitions: An automaton here is a finite transition system \(A=(Q,\Sigma ,\delta )\), with |\(Q|=n, a\) finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), and a total function \(\delta :Q\times \Sigma \to Q\). Extend \(\delta\) to words by \(\delta (q,\varepsilon )=q\) and \(\delta (q,wa)=\delta (\delta (q,w),a)\). A word w is a reset word when |\(\{\delta (q,w):q\in Q\}|=1\). The automaton is synchronizing if at least one such word exists; its reset threshold \(rt(A)\) is the minimum number of letters in a reset word. The quantification ranges over every n and every finite alphabet and total transition function satisfying this promise. The common final state need not be specified beforehand. Initial states and accepting states play no role. The empty word handles \(n=1\). No strong-connectivity, binary-alphabet, permutation-letter, or other structural restriction is imposed. Partial automata, nondeterministic transitions, and synchronizing only a prescribed proper subset of Q are different models. The maximum is well-defined: on n labeled states there are only \(n^{n}\) different letter transformations, and duplicate transformations may be removed without changing shortest reset lengths. Thus finitely many transition alphabets suffice. \(T(1)=0\). The target is the integer-valued function of n, not the running time of testing synchronization.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real-valued approximation g on the positive integers and prove in Lean that |\(g(n)- (T(n) : \mathbb{R} )|\le 1/100\) for every integer \(n\ge 1\), using the model and target defined here. Certified lower and upper functions \(\ell\)\((n)\le T(n)\le u(n)\) with \(u(n)- \ell (n)\le 1/50\) also qualify via their midpoint. The answer may use unambiguous mathematical expressions or certified bounds; g need not be integer-valued, and no simple exact formula for \(T(n)\) is required. An exact determination also qualifies. A one-sided bound, agreement at finitely many n, or an asymptotic estimate without the stated pointwise error guarantee does not meet this criterion.

cards.title: Sakoda–Sipser problem
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(C,k\ge 1\) exist such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every finite nonempty input alphabet \(\Sigma\) and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over \(\Sigma\) with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states satisfying \(\mathrm{L}(D)=\mathrm{L}(A)\)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
cards.definitions: The read-only input tape contains a left endmarker, a word \(w\in \Sigma\)*, and a right endmarker. Each automaton has one head, initially on the left endmarker, a finite set Q of states with a designated initial state and designated halting accepting states. In each nonhalting configuration it uses its current state and the scanned symbol to choose a new state and a head displacement in \(\{- 1,0,+1\}\); moves outside the endmarkers are forbidden. A missing transition rejects that branch. A word is accepted if some finite computation reaches an accepting state. Infinite nonaccepting branches do not count as acceptance. For a deterministic automaton there is at most one available transition in each state-symbol pair, and its unique infinite run, if any, rejects. There is no work tape, rewritable input, second head, stack, counter, randomness or advice. State count includes all control and halting states, but the bound is independent of word length and alphabet size. The target is existence of D for each A; computing D from A is not required to take polynomial time. Standard endmarker and stay-put conventions change these state bounds only by polynomial factors.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of universal constants C,k giving an equivalent 2DFA with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states for every n-state 2NFA, or prove that no such constants exist. In the negative direction, every proposed polynomial bound must fail on some source automaton; all language comparisons concern words of every length.

cards.title: Generalized star-height problem
cards.formal: Does there exist a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\) and a regular language \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \Sigma\)* such that every generalized regular expression denoting L has Kleene-star nesting depth at least two, when complement is allowed without increasing that depth?
cards.definitions: \(\Sigma\)* is the set of all finite words over \(\Sigma\), including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). A regular language is one accepted by a finite deterministic automaton. Generalized expressions are finite expressions built from \(\varnothing , \varepsilon\), and the letters \(a\in \Sigma\) using binary union \(E\cup F\), concatenation EF, complement \(E^{c}\), and Kleene star E*. Their meanings are respectively the empty language, \(\{\varepsilon\}, \{a\}\), language union, all concatenations uv with \(u\in \mathrm{L}(E)\) and \(v\in \mathrm{L}(F), \Sigma *\setminus \mathrm{L}(E)\), and the union of all finite concatenation powers of \(\mathrm{L}(E)\), including power zero \(\{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(h(\varnothing )=h(\varepsilon )=h(a)=0, h(E\cup F)=h(\mathrm{EF})=\max \{h(E),h(F)\}, h(E^{c})=h(E)\), and \(h(E*)=h(E)+1\). Define \(h_{g}(\mathrm{L})=\min \{h(E):\mathrm{L}(E)=\mathrm{L}\}\), which exists because every regular language has an ordinary regular expression. The question is whether \(h_{g}(\mathrm{L})>1\) for at least one such L. There is no bound on expression size, number of complements, union or concatenation depth, automaton size, or alphabet size. Intersection is permitted as the abbreviation \((E^{c}\cup F^{c})^{c}\) and does not add star depth. Backreferences, infinite words, additional predicates and auxiliary alphabets in the final expression are not part of the syntax.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some regular language has generalized star height at least two, including a lower bound over all generalized expressions for that language, or prove that every regular language over every finite nonempty alphabet has a generalized expression of star height at most one. Expression size is unrestricted in both alternatives.
cards.status_note: The checked author sources distinguish the open generalized question from the solved ordinary star-height problem. A later-work search on 11 September 2026 found no verified height-two example or universal height-one theorem. The inspected factor-counting results establish additional height-one subclasses only.

cards.title: Decidability of every level of the dot-depth hierarchy
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), is there an algorithm that, given a deterministic finite automaton over a finite alphabet A, always halts and decides whether its language belongs to \(DD_{k}(A)\), the k-th dot-depth level defined below?
cards.definitions: For each finite nonempty alphabet A, let A* be its finite words, \(\varepsilon\) the empty word, and \(A+=A*\setminus \{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(DD_{0}(A)=\{\varnothing ,\{\varepsilon\},A+,A*\}\). For a class C of languages over \(A, Pol(C)\) consists of all finite unions of marked products \(\mathrm{L}_{0}a_{1}\mathrm{L}_{1}\cdots a_{r} \mathrm{L}_{r}\), where \(r\ge 0\), each \(a_{i}\in A\), and every \(\mathrm{L}_{i}\in C; r=0\) gives \(\mathrm{L}_{0}\). Let \(Bool(C)\) be closure under finite union, finite intersection and complement relative to A*. Define \(DD_{k+1}(A)\)=Bool(\(Pol(DD_{k}(A))\)). The input automaton is given by finite explicit tables, including its alphabet, initial state and accepting states; its accepted language is \(\mathrm{L}(M)\). The question quantifies \(\forall k\exists a\) total Turing algorithm \(A_{k}\forall M\), with \(A_{k}(M)\)=yes exactly when \(\mathrm{L}(M)\in DD_{k}(A)\). Each \(A_{k}\) must handle arbitrary finite input alphabets. No polynomial-time or elementary-time bound is requested. This fixes the full integer levels and the four-language level-zero convention; it does not merge distinct concatenation hierarchies or leave the logical signature implicit. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that membership in \(DD_{k}\) is decidable for every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), with each decider handling all finite alphabets, or prove that membership is undecidable for at least one fixed level k. The positive statement does not require an effective procedure that takes k as an additional input.

cards.title: Equivalence of deterministic macro tree transducers
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given two deterministic macro tree transducers with the same finite ranked input and output alphabets, decides whether they define exactly the same partial function from finite ordered input trees to finite ordered output trees?
cards.definitions: Fix the ordinary inside-out, or call-by-value, semantics. A ranked alphabet assigns a nonnegative arity to each symbol; a tree node has exactly that many ordered children. A transducer has finitely many states q, each with one input-tree argument and \(m(q)\) output-tree parameters, and an initial state \(q_{0}\) with \(m(q_{0})=0\). For each state q and input symbol \(\sigma\) of arity k there is at most one rule \(q(\sigma (x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k}),y_{1},\ldots ,y_{m})\to r\). The finite right-hand side follows the grammar \(r ::= y_{j} | \delta (r_{1},\ldots ,r_{l}) | q' (x_{i},r_{1},\ldots ,r_{m(q' )})\), with \(\delta\) an output symbol of arity l and \(1\le i\le k\). Subtrees and parameters may be copied or deleted, and calls may be nested inside parameter arguments without a fixed nesting bound across instances. On input \(\sigma (t_{1},\ldots ,t_{k})\), evaluate parameter arguments to output trees, then evaluate a call \(q'\) on the indicated child \(t_{i}\) with those parameter values. A missing rule makes the corresponding evaluation undefined, and under call-by-value an undefined argument makes its enclosing evaluation undefined. There is no inspection or pattern matching on parameter trees. Every recursive call processes a proper input child, so evaluation terminates on each finite input, with either a finite tree or undefined. A transducer with a rule for every state/symbol pair is total. There is no regular look-ahead oracle in this chosen syntax. Equality requires identical domains and, on that domain, identical labelled ordered output trees, without identifying different trees by their leaf strings, shapes or origin annotations. Input alphabets, state sets, arities and rules are all part of the finite input to the desired decision algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that equivalence of the specified partial deterministic macro tree transducers is decidable by a total algorithm, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. Equivalence requires equality of domains and of the labelled ordered output trees on every input in the common domain.

The inspected 2025–2026 papers classify shape, growth or expressive power. Their claims do not decide ordinary functional equivalence of arbitrary pairs.

cards.title: Positivity problem for linear recurrences
cards.formal: Does there exist a Turing machine that, on every input consisting of an integer \(d\ge 1\), integer initial values \(u_{0},\ldots ,u_{d- 1}\), and integer coefficients \(a_{0},\ldots ,a_{d- 1}\), halts and decides whether \(u_{n}\ge 0\) for every \(n\ge 0\), where \(u_{n+d}=\sum _{i=0}^{d- 1}a_{i} u_{n+i}\)? The order d is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound.
cards.definitions: All integers are given exactly in signed binary, and the coefficient and initial-value lists are explicit. The recurrence is homogeneous and its coefficients are constant in n. The requested property includes every term from \(u_{0}\) onward and allows zero terms. Coefficients may be zero, including \(a_{0}\); the decision procedure must accept these inputs as well. No promise of distinct characteristic roots, reversibility, eventual nonnegativity, or bounded order is imposed. The recurrence supplied need not be of minimal order. Computation uses the ordinary Turing model, with no real-number or number-theoretic oracle. No polynomial-time or other specified running-time bound is required, but the machine must halt for both possible answers. A simple sequence has a minimal characteristic polynomial with no repeated complex roots. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that nonnegativity of every term is decidable for integer linear recurrences of arbitrary input order, by a machine halting on both positive and negative instances, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. The property is \(u_{n}\ge 0\) for all \(n\ge 0\), including the initial values.

cards.title: Simple stochastic games in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is the following decision problem in deterministic polynomial time? Given an explicitly represented finite simple stochastic game G, a start vertex s, and a binary rational threshold \(r\in [0,1]\), decide whether \(v_{G}(s)>r\), where \(v_{G}(s)=\sup _{\sigma} \inf _{\tau} \Pr _{s}^{\sigma ,\tau}\)[eventually reach the target sink 1]. The game and threshold follow the exact conventions below, and time is polynomial in their total bit length.
cards.definitions: The vertices are partitioned into Max, Min, random, and two distinct terminal sinks 0 and 1. Every nonterminal vertex has two listed successor slots; slots may have the same successor. At a Max or Min vertex its owner chooses a slot. At a random vertex each slot is chosen with probability \(1/2\), independently at each visit. Both players observe the complete finite history and the current vertex. Strategies may use history and private randomness; there is no bound on play length. Reaching 1 gives Max payoff one; reaching 0, or playing forever without reaching 1, gives payoff zero. Min minimizes the same expected payoff that Max maximizes. No promise of almost-sure termination is imposed. All vertices, ownership labels and successor indices are explicit; \(r=a/b\) is exact with binary integers \(0\le a\le b\) and \(b>0\). Equality \(v_{G}(s)=r\) is a NO instance. The algorithm is an ordinary uniform deterministic Turing algorithm; its polynomial bound has universal constants independent of the game and threshold. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the exact threshold language \(\{(G,s,r):v_{G}(s)>r\}\) belongs to P, or prove that it does not. The polynomial-time algorithm must handle arbitrary finite games, including nonterminating plays, and reject equality to the threshold.
cards.status_note: Rechecked on 11 September 2026. The inspected 2026 work on iteration and stopping ladder games does not give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for all exact threshold instances. No resolution was located in the later-work search.

cards.title: Internal semisimplicial types in ordinary HoTT
cards.formal: In the fixed ordinary HoTT theory T below, can one define a single internal family \(S:\mathbb{N} \to U_{1}\) and restriction maps \(r_{n}:S(n+1)\to S(n)\) whose finite stages are equivalent, compatibly with restriction, to the canonical finite semisimplicial telescopes \(D_{n}\)?
cards.definitions: Fix T to be intensional Martin–Löf type theory with dependent function and pair types \(\Pi ,\Sigma\), identity types with their J eliminator, empty and unit types, finite coproducts, natural numbers and W-types, a cumulative predicative sequence \(U_{0}:U_{1}:\cdots\) closed under these constructors, and univalence for these universes. Also allow propositional truncation and homotopy pushouts with their ordinary dependent eliminators and propositional computation rules for path constructors, as in the HoTT book. There is no equality reflection, axiom K/UIP, resizing, choice, excluded middle, second equality type, display modality, or additional primitive for semisimplicial types. The question concerns definability in this specified theory; a negative result would apply to this theory, not automatically to every possible extension called HoTT. Define an external, finite family of syntactic telescopes as follows. \(D_{0}\) is \(U_{0}\), with element \(A_{0}\). Given data \(d=(A_{0},\ldots ,A_{j- 1})\) in \(D_{j- 1}\), form \(B_{j}(d)\), the dependent type of labelled boundaries of a j-simplex: for every nonempty proper subset F of \(\{0,\ldots ,j\}\), in increasing cardinality and then lexicographic order, choose a label \(x_{F}\) in \(A_{|F|- 1}\) evaluated on the labels of all nonempty proper subfaces of F. Identify F with \(\{0,\ldots ,|F|- 1\}\) by its increasing enumeration when supplying these arguments. For singleton F this means \(x_{F}:A_{0}\). Set \(D_{j}=\Sigma (d:D_{j- 1})(B_{j}(d)\to U_{0})\), whose last field is \(A_{j}\), and let \(p_{j}:D_{j+1}\to D_{j}\) forget the last field. This describes an ordinary finite T-expression for each external integer j; it does not postulate an internal function \(j\mapsto D_{j}\). The required output is finite closed T-terms \(S:\mathbb{N} \to U_{1}\) and \(r:\Pi (n:\mathbb{N} )(S(n+1)\to S(n))\), together with a metatheoretic proof that for every external j there are T-terms \(e_{j}:S(j)\)≃\(D_{j}\) and homotopies \(e_{j}\circ r_{j} \sim  p_{j}\circ e_{j+1}\). Here j inside T denotes its numeral, ≃ is the usual type equivalence, and ~ is pointwise identity. No judgmental equality between \(S(j)\) and \(D_{j}\) is required. The equivalences classify the full type-valued telescopes, with arbitrary \(U_{0}\)-small simplex types and no fixed truncation bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the specified theory T admits finite closed terms S and r together with the external stagewise equivalences and compatibility homotopies required above, or prove that no such terms and witnesses exist in T. The positive conclusion must hold at every external finite stage and allow arbitrary \(U_{0}\)-small simplex types.

cards.title: Scott-continuous lambda models with theory \(\lambda \beta\)
cards.formal: Does there exist a pointed directed-complete partial order D and Scott-continuous maps \(F:D\to [D\to D]\) and \(\mathrm{L}:[D\to D]\to D\) with \(F\circ \mathrm{L}=id\) such that, for every pair of finite untyped lambda terms M,N, equality of their interpretations for every environment in D holds if and only if M and N are beta-convertible?
cards.definitions: Terms are generated by variables from a countably infinite set, application MN and abstraction \(\lambda x\).M, modulo renaming bound variables. Beta-convertibility is the least equivalence relation closed under application and abstraction containing (\(\lambda x\).M)\(N=M[N/x]\), with capture-avoiding substitution. A directed set is nonempty and every two of its elements have an upper bound in the set. D is a set with a partial order, a least element, and a supremum for every directed subset. Scott-continuous means monotone and preserving directed suprema. \([D\to D]\) consists of all Scott-continuous functions, ordered pointwise. An environment \(\rho\) assigns an element of D to each variable. Interpret x as \(\rho (x), MN\) as F(⟦M⟧\(\rho\))(⟦N⟧\(\rho\)), and \(\lambda x\).M as L(\(d\mapsto\)⟦M⟧\((\rho [x:=d])\)). The desired condition is \(\forall M,N\): (\(\forall \rho\), ⟦M⟧\(\rho\)=⟦N⟧\(\rho\)) ⇔ \(M=\beta N\). Models need not be countable, algebraic, effectively presented or extensional; in particular \(\mathrm{L}\circ F=id\) is not required. These are set-based directed-complete orders and all their continuous maps, without a restriction to graph models.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that a pointed dcpo and continuous retraction F,L satisfying the stated exact-theory condition exist, or prove that none exist. A negative answer must cover all such dcpos, without assuming an effective presentation, algebraicity or extensionality.
cards.status_note: The exact question is explicit in Honsell’s primary statement. A search through 11 September 2026 found no resolution of its \(\lambda \beta\) alternative. The inspected 2025–2026 filter-model papers study unsolvables and other equational theories. Proofs were not independently verified.

cards.title: Barendregt–Geuvers–Klop conjecture
cards.formal: For every pure type system \((S,A,R)\) defined below, does weak normalization of every typable term imply strong normalization of every typable term?
cards.definitions: S is a set of sorts, \(A\subseteq S\times S\) is a set of axioms, and \(R\subseteq S\times S\times S\) is a set of product rules. Terms are finite expressions \(t ::= x | s | t u | \lambda x:B\).\(t | \Pi x:B\).C, with \(s\in S\) and variables from a countably infinite set, modulo renaming bound variables. A context is a finite sequence of declarations of distinct variables. Typing is the least relation \(\Gamma \vdash t:B\) generated by the following rules. Axiom: \(\varnothing \vdash s:t\) when \((s,t)\in A\). Start: \(\Gamma ,x:B\vdash x:B\) when \(\Gamma \vdash B:s\) and x is fresh. Weakening: \(\Gamma ,x:C\vdash t:B\) when \(\Gamma \vdash t:B, \Gamma \vdash C:s\) and x is fresh. Product: \(\Gamma \vdash \Pi x:B\).\(C:s_{3}\) when \(\Gamma \vdash B:s_{1}, \Gamma ,x:B\vdash C:s_{2}\) and \((s_{1},s_{2},s_{3})\in R\). Abstraction: \(\Gamma \vdash \lambda x:B\).\(t:\Pi x:B\).C when \(\Gamma ,x:B\vdash t:C\) and \(\Gamma \vdash \Pi x:B\).C:s for a sort s. Application: \(\Gamma \vdash t u:C[u/x]\) when \(\Gamma \vdash t:\Pi x:B\).C and \(\Gamma \vdash u:B\). Conversion: \(\Gamma \vdash t:C\) when \(\Gamma \vdash t:B, \Gamma \vdash C:s\) and \(B=\beta C\). All substitutions avoid capture. A beta step contracts (\(\lambda x:B\).t)u to \(t[u/x]\) at any subterm, including inside annotations and product types. =\(\beta\) is the reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure of those steps. A term is typable if \(\Gamma \vdash t:B\) for some finite \(\Gamma ,B\). Weak normalization means that each typable term has some finite beta-reduction sequence ending in a term with no beta redex. Strong normalization means that no typable term starts an infinite beta-reduction sequence. Both predicates quantify over open as well as closed terms and over all their reduction choices. The sets S,A,R need not be finite, decidable or functional.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every pure type system in which all typable terms are weakly beta-normalizing is strongly beta-normalizing, or exhibit a pure type system that is weakly normalizing for every typable term but has a typable term admitting an infinite beta-reduction sequence.
cards.status_note: The primary statement and Mull’s 2023 paper leave the unrestricted conjecture open. A later-result and author-publication search on 11 September 2026 found no general proof or counterexample. The positive theorems impose additional PTS structure.

cards.title: P versus NC
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NC}\), where NC consists of decision languages recognized by logspace-uniform Boolean circuit families of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have such a circuit family?
cards.definitions: P is deterministic polynomial time on ordinary Turing machines. For \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{NC}\) there must be fixed constants c,k,C and a family \((C_{n})_{n}\ge 0\) such that \(C_{n}\) decides membership in L correctly on every n-bit input, has at most \(C(n+2)^{c}\) gates, and has depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{k}\). Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; fan-out is unrestricted and one output bit is designated. Depth is the longest input-to-output gate path. A deterministic \(O(\log (n+2))\)-space transducer given \(1^{n}\) must output the description of \(C_{n}\); its polynomial output bound is part of the size requirement. Constants and the generator may depend on L but not on n. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered Boolean gate DAG, its input-bit values, and an output-gate index; it asks whether that gate evaluates to 1. Its input length n is the entire binary encoding length, and malformed encodings are rejected. No randomization, advice, oracle, or restriction to monotone gates is permitted. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every language in P has a logspace-uniform family of polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth circuits, or prove that some language in P has no such family. By the stated completeness result, the affirmative answer is equivalent to Circuit Value belonging to NC, and the negative answer to Circuit Value not belonging to NC. Excluding only one fixed depth exponent, nonuniform monotone circuits, or one evaluation procedure does not establish \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NC}\).
cards.status_note: The primary P-completeness monograph and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No unrestricted resolution of P versus logspace-uniform NC was found. The \(2025/2026\) matching lower bound concerns monotone circuits and therefore does not resolve the stated \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) model.

cards.title: Directed reachability with nearly linear memory and polylogarithmic passes
cards.formal: Do there exist constants a,b,C and a uniform randomized streaming algorithm that decides directed s–t reachability on every n-vertex graph using at most \(Cn(\log (n+2))^{a}\) bits of memory and \(C(\log (n+2))^{b}\) passes, with success probability at least \(2/3\) for every adversarially ordered edge stream?
cards.definitions: The input is a finite simple directed graph on the labelled vertex set \([n], n\ge 2\), with distinct designated vertices s,t. The algorithm knows n,s,t before reading the edges. Each directed edge occurs once in an insertion-only stream, in an arbitrary order fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits. Each pass scans this same stream in the same forward order. The input is read-only: there are no adjacency queries, random-access reads, sorting operations on external storage, or writable auxiliary streams. All mutable working storage counts toward the bit bound; fresh independent random bits may be read from a one-way random source. The memory and pass bounds hold on every execution. Computation between successive input items is unrestricted but must terminate; no running-time bound beyond termination is imposed. A yes answer means that there is a directed path from s to t in the input graph. The constants and algorithm are independent of n, the graph, and the edge order.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that one uniform randomized decision algorithm has simultaneous \(O(n \log ^{a}(n+2))\)-bit space and \(O(\log ^{b}(n+2))\)-pass bounds for fixed constants a,b on every execution, and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every fixed graph and edge order. Alternatively, prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. Ruling out a fixed pass count, requiring the output of a path, or restricting computation between stream items does not establish the stated negation.
cards.status_note: The primary survey, cited multipass bounds and the revision of 9 September 2026 were checked on 11 September 2026. The recent paper explicitly retains the \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\)-pass upper benchmark. No polylogarithmic-pass algorithm or lower bound ruling out every polylogarithmic pass bound in the stated memory model was found. This check covers decision with adversarial fixed order, rather than a changed stream or a path-output requirement.

cards.title: Perfect matching in NC
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C,a,b>0\) and a logspace-uniform family of Boolean circuits which, on the adjacency matrix of every n-vertex simple undirected graph, output a perfect matching or correctly report that none exists, with at most \(C(n+2)^{a}\) gates and depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{b}\)?
cards.definitions: The input is the \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix of a graph on \([n]\), with symmetry and zero diagonal promised. A perfect matching is a set of edges with exactly one edge incident to each vertex. Output is a flag and an \(n\times n\) binary incidence matrix for the chosen matching; when the flag reports nonexistence the remaining output bits are ignored. The empty graph has the empty perfect matching. Circuits use fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\), fan-in-one NOT, constants 0,1 and unrestricted fan-out. Depth counts gates on the longest input-output path and size counts gates; the \(n^{2}\) output positions are specified as part of the description. A deterministic Turing transducer on unary input \(1^{n}\) writes the description using \(O(\log _{2}(n+2))\) work bits, with read-only input and write-only output. Constants and generator are fixed across n; every valid input must receive an exact answer. No randomness, oracle, advice, bipartiteness or other structural graph promise is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of the stated logspace-uniform polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth search circuits on all simple undirected graphs, or prove that no such family exists. A negative answer rules out every fixed choice of the size and depth exponents and constants. An algorithm only for bipartite graphs, or one using quasipolynomial circuit size or catalytic auxiliary memory, does not meet the specified positive criterion.

cards.title: Distributed Lovász Local Lemma in \(O(\log  \log  n)\) rounds
cards.formal: Does there exist an integer \(c\ge 2\) such that, for every fixed integer \(d\ge 2, a\) uniform randomized LOCAL algorithm \(A_{d}\) and a constant \(K_{d}\) solve every n-event variable Lovász Local Lemma instance of dependency degree at most d and maximum bad-event probability p with \(p\cdot d^{c}<1/2\), within \(K_{d}(1+\log _{2}\log _{2}(n+2))\) rounds, with probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\) of avoiding all bad events simultaneously?
cards.definitions: There are \(n\ge 2\) bad events, each a predicate on a specified finite subset of finitely many mutually independent variables. Each variable has a finite nonempty alphabet and a rational probability distribution; event predicates and distributions are given by finite tables. Variables occurring in no event can be omitted. Two distinct event nodes are adjacent exactly when their variable sets intersect; this graph is the communication network. Its maximum degree is at most d. The number p is the largest probability of an event under the product of the specified distributions. Each node initially knows n,d, its own event table, its variables and their distributions, its neighbours and their identifiers. Node identifiers are distinct integers in \([n^{2}]\); shared variables have consistent names. LOCAL means synchronous rounds with arbitrarily long finite messages in each direction on each edge, and unrestricted terminating local computation. Nodes have private independent fair random bits. A single finite program is used at all nodes, independently of n and the instance. Each node outputs one value for each of its variables. Success requires agreement on shared variables and falsity of every event. The round bound holds on every random tape; the success probability is over all node coins for each fixed instance and identifier assignment. Constants and the algorithm may depend on d; the slack exponent c is chosen before d. No preprocessing using the full instance is supplied. The factor \(1/2\) removes the low-degree ambiguity recorded in the source conjecture.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed integer \(c\ge 2\) admits, for every fixed \(d\ge 2\), algorithms \(A_{d}\) and constants \(K_{d}\) with the stated round and global-success bounds on all eligible instances. Alternatively, prove that for every candidate c there is a fixed d for which no such algorithm and constant exist. An obstruction at one slack exponent alone does not refute the existential choice of c. Bounds averaged over nodes, expected round bounds, or a higher fixed power of log log n do not meet the stated guarantee.
cards.status_note: The original conjecture, primary distributed bounds, the 2025 locality result and the August 2026 resilient-LLL paper were checked on 11 September 2026. No result settling the exact bounded-degree \(O(\log  \log  n)\) worst-case target was found. The fixed factor \(1/2\) and order of slack/degree quantifiers preserve the saved precise interpretation. Node averages and results for stronger communication models are not substituted for this guarantee.

cards.title: Optimal exact single-source shortest paths in CONGEST
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(b\ge 1\), do there exist constants \(K,c>0\) and a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm which, on every connected simple undirected graph with \(n\ge 2\) vertices, integer edge weights in \([0,n^{b}]\) and a designated source s, makes every vertex output its exact weighted distance from s in at most \(K(\sqrt{n}+D)(\log _{2}(n+2))^{c}\) rounds on every execution, with simultaneous correctness probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\)? Here D is the diameter of the unweighted graph.
cards.definitions: A path length is the sum of its edge weights; the distance is the minimum path length, and the source distance is zero. D is the maximum over vertex pairs of the minimum number of edges on a path between them. The graph itself is the network. In each synchronous round, each endpoint of each edge can send at most \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits to the other endpoint, for a constant B depending only on b. Nodes initially know n,b, the source identifier, their own identifiers, and the identifiers and weights of incident neighbours. Identifiers are distinct integers in \([n^{2}]\). Local computation and memory are unrestricted, but each local computation between rounds terminates. Nodes use independent private fair random bits. One finite program, allowed to depend on b, runs at all nodes; no global graph description, advice, routing tables or preprocessing is supplied. The graph, weights, source and identifiers are fixed before randomness is drawn. Output at v is an ordinary binary integer for \(\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\), stored locally. The guarantee concerns all vertices together, over all coins. All communication, including finding termination and any preprocessing, counts in the round bound. K,c,B are independent of n,D and the instance; no value of D is initially supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed weight exponent b there is a single uniform algorithm meeting the stated \(O((\sqrt{n}+D)\operatorname{polylog} n)\) round bound on every execution and the simultaneous \(1- n^{- 3}\) correctness probability on every eligible network. Alternatively, prove that this is impossible for at least one fixed b, for every choice of algorithm and fixed constants K,c,B. An approximation guarantee, an \(n^{o(1)}\) overhead not bounded by a fixed power of log n, or a result for only one diameter regime is not the stated affirmative answer.

cards.title: Strongly polynomial linear programming
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm, with fixed polynomials p and q, that solves every rational linear program $\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}$, where A has m rows and n columns, using at most \(p(m+n)\) elementary arithmetic, comparison, and data-transfer operations, while every intermediate rational number has binary encoding length at most \(q(N)\)? Here N is the total input bit length. Solving means returning an exact optimal rational solution if one exists, or correctly reporting infeasibility or an objective unbounded below.
cards.definitions: A is in \(\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\), b in \(\mathbb{Q}^{m}\), and c in \(\mathbb{Q}^{n}\), with \(m,n\ge 1\). All coefficients are supplied explicitly as binary signed numerators and positive denominators. No full-rank, nondegeneracy, strict-feasibility, coefficient-size, or conditioning promise is made. Elementary scalar operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero quantity, comparisons, and transfers of stored values. The program is fixed and finite; no oracle, advice, randomization, floor operation, or uncharged access to binary digits is allowed. Rational encoding length means the bit length of a numerator-denominator representation. The polynomial p is independent of N and of every coefficient magnitude; q may depend on N. Consequently the algorithm must also admit a polynomial-time bit implementation. The output is a solution vector, not a required optimal basis. Infeasible means that the feasible set is empty; unbounded means it is nonempty and the infimum of \(c^{T} x\) is minus infinity. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.status_note: The standard problem remains listed as open, but a direct claimed solution exists in Awoniyi’s July 2026 revision. This card records it without treating it as established: correctness, the iteration bound, and the full strongly polynomial guarantee have not been independently validated in this review. Checked through 10 September 2026.

cards.title: Exact semidefinite feasibility in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is the following language in P in the ordinary Turing model: all lists of symmetric rational matrices \(A_{0},A_{1},\ldots ,A_{m}\in Q^{n\times n}\) for which there exists a real vector \(x\in R^{m}\) satisfying \(A_{0}+\sum _{i=1}^{m} x_{i} A_{i}\succeq 0\)? Both m and n are unbounded parts of the input, and the algorithm must decide exact nonemptiness in time polynomial in the total binary encoding length.
cards.definitions: Every matrix entry is an explicitly supplied rational number, with signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator; all matrices have the same size \(n\ge 1\). A symmetric matrix M is positive semidefinite, written \(M\succeq 0\), when \(z^{T}Mz\ge 0\) for every real vector z, equivalently when all eigenvalues are nonnegative. The unknown x ranges over all real vectors, not just rational vectors. Singular feasible matrices count as YES. There is no strict-feasibility, boundedness, conditioning, rank, or distance-to-infeasibility promise, and no radius or accuracy parameter is supplied. The output is one bit specifying whether any feasible x exists; an explicit feasible point is not required. An affine subspace given by rational linear equations can be parametrized by rational Gaussian elimination, so this is also the rational-affine-subspace intersection formulation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The primary literature retains general exact SDP feasibility as an open polynomial-time problem. Ramana’s dual does not establish \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) membership in the Turing model, and recent convex-polynomial optimization results address a different constraint family. This card permits real witnesses, singular feasible points, weak infeasibility and unbounded feasible regions.

cards.title: Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite clutter with the packing property have the max-flow min-cut property? Equivalently, if every deletion/contraction minor satisfies unweighted integral packing–covering equality, must weighted integral packing–covering equality hold for every nonnegative integer weight vector?
cards.definitions:
A clutter \(\mathcal C\) on a finite ground set \(E\) is a family of subsets of \(E\), no one properly containing another. Its original members are nonempty; the empty family is allowed. A cover is a set \(T\subseteq E\) meeting every member, and \(	au(\mathcal C)\) is its minimum cardinality. A packing is a family of pairwise disjoint members; \(
u(\mathcal C)\) is its maximum cardinality. Deleting an element removes it from the ground set and discards all members containing it. Contracting an element removes it from the ground set and from every member, then keeps only inclusion-minimal members. A minor is obtained by any finite sequence of these operations, including the empty sequence. The packing property is \(	au(\mathcal D)=
u(\mathcal D)\) for every minor \(\mathcal D\). For the empty family both numbers are zero. For the degenerate minor \(\{\varnothing\}\), set both numbers to \(+\infty\): no cover exists and arbitrarily many copies of the empty member can be packed. These conventions give no obstruction from degenerate minors. For an original clutter and capacities \(w\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{E}\), define \[	au_w(\mathcal C)=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in T}w_e:T\subseteq E	ext{ is a cover}ight\},\qquad 
u_w(\mathcal C)=\max\left\{\sum_{F\in\mathcal C}y_F:y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{\mathcal C},\ \sum_{F
i e}y_F\le w_e	ext{ for every }e\in Eight\}.\] Multiplicities \(y_F\) allow repeated packed members, and every copy consumes one unit of capacity at each of its elements. Both optima are finite because original members are nonempty. The max-flow min-cut (MFMC) property is equality of these optima for every nonnegative integer capacity vector; the weights and ground-set size have no fixed upper bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal implication, or of its logical negation. An affirmative answer must establish \(\tau_w(\mathcal C)=\nu_w(\mathcal C)\) for every clutter with the packing property and every nonnegative integer vector \(w\). A negative answer must exhibit a finite clutter and such a vector with \(\tau_w(\mathcal C)>\nu_w(\mathcal C)\), and verify the packing property for every minor. A finite census, a proper subclass theorem, or fractional duality alone is insufficient.
cards.status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. Abdi–Schwarcz v2 (9 July 2026) explicitly retains the general conjecture and reports verification on at most ten elements. Roy–Saha v2 treats only (n−2)-uniform clutters. No general resolution was located in the bounded search; neither the computational artifacts nor these source proofs were independently verified.

cards.title: Nearly linear-time solution of general sparse linear systems
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(c\ge 1\), does there exist a uniform randomized classical algorithm \(A_{c}\) with the following guarantee? Given \(n\ge 2, a\) nonsingular rational \(n\times n\) matrix A with m nonzero entries, a nonzero rational vector b, and an integer \(1\le p\le c\cdot \operatorname{ceil}(\log _{2} n)\), output a rational vector x̂ such that ||\(A\hat\{x\}- b||_{2}\le 2^{- p}||b||_{2}\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Each numerator and positive denominator of A and b has at most \(c\cdot \operatorname{ceil}(\log _{2} n)\) binary digits, and the spectral condition number \(\kappa _{2}(A)\) is promised at most \(n^{c}\). The worst-case running time must be \(O_{c}(m \log ^{d_{c}}n)\) for some constant \(d_{c}\) independent of the input.
cards.definitions: The input lists the row index, column index and rational value of each nonzero coefficient, without duplicate positions, together with the n entries of b; hence \(n\le m\le n^{2}\). The Euclidean norm is ||\(v||_{2}=(\sum_{i} v_{i}^{2})^{1/2}\), and \(\kappa _{2}(A)=\sigma _{\mathrm{max}}(A)/\sigma _{\mathrm{min}}(A)\), the ratio of its largest and smallest singular values. Nonsingularity makes the denominator positive. A may be nonsymmetric, indefinite and unrelated to a graph Laplacian. The algorithm need only meet its guarantee on promised inputs; it is not asked to certify the condition-number promise. Computation uses a word RAM with \(\Theta (\log  n)\)-bit words, conventional arithmetic, comparison, bit operations and memory access; all operations on longer numbers, preprocessing, random-bit generation and writing the output are charged. No operation on an arbitrary real number has unit cost. Converting word operations to bit operations changes only polylogarithmic factors. Constants and the fixed program may depend on c, but neither nonuniform advice depending on n nor a supplied inverse or preconditioner is allowed. Here \(\varepsilon =2^{- p}\); this is the polynomial-condition, inverse-polynomial-accuracy regime of the near-input-size target. The output is the full list of n rational coordinates, each as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator; every output bit is charged. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) (or \(\Theta (\log  N)\) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

The faster-than-matrix-multiplication problem has already been solved. The August 2026 report discusses broader scalable solvers but does not claim this universal guarantee; the simplicial-Laplacian reduction is not a general running-time lower bound.

cards.title: Smale’s seventh problem
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants \(C,K>0\), an integer \(k\ge1\), and one deterministic real-number algorithm \(A\) in the model below such that, for every integer \(N\ge2\), \(A(N)\) outputs distinct points \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\in S^2\) in at most \(KN^k\) operations and satisfies \(E_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\le E_N^{\ast}+C\ln N\)?
cards.definitions: Let \(S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2=1\}\). For distinct points define \(E_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=-\sum_{i\ne j}\ln\|x_i-x_j\|_2\), counting ordered pairs; configurations with collisions have energy \(+\infty\). Let \(E_N^{\ast}\) be the infimum over all \(N\)-tuples on \(S^2\). Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm and \(\|\cdot\|_2\) is Euclidean distance. Use one deterministic finite real-arithmetic program with a fixed finite list of real constants independent of \(N\). The machine has exact real registers, finite control and tapes; each scalar copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero register, sign test, or tape movement costs one operation. It may allocate storage, charging the operations that use it, and has no primitive logarithm, square root, floor, randomness or optimization oracle. The input integer \(N\) is supplied as one exact real value. Output is the explicit list of \(3N\) coordinates, all required to lie exactly on the sphere. Time is polynomial in \(N\), not in \(\log N\); this is a real-number computation model, not a bit-cost model. The energy inequality is a mathematical condition on the output, and the machine need not evaluate that energy.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of one permitted real-arithmetic program and constants \(C,K,k\), independent of \(N\), satisfying both the time and energy guarantees for every integer \(N\ge2\), or prove in Lean that no such program and constants exist. The output must lie exactly on the sphere. Expected energy under a distribution, finitely many solved cardinalities, or a larger asymptotic additive error does not meet this criterion.

cards.title: Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist a real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every isotropic log-concave probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and every locally Lipschitz function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) with \(\int f^2\,d\mu<\infty\) and \(\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu<\infty\), \[\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)\le C\int_{\mathbb R^n}\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)?\] The same constant must work for all dimensions, measures and admissible functions. This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
cards.definitions: All norms and derivatives are Euclidean, with \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^{1/2}\). Here a log-concave probability measure has a Lebesgue density \(\rho(x)=e^{-V(x)}\) of integral one, where \(V:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is measurable and convex; \(e^{-\infty}=0\). Convexity means \(V((1-s)x+sy)\le(1-s)V(x)+sV(y)\) for all \(x,y\) and \(0<s<1\), using the extended-real convention on the right. Thus \(d\mu(x)=\rho(x)\,dx\). Isotropy means finite second moments and \(\int x_i\,d\mu=0\), \(\int x_i x_j\,d\mu=\delta_{ij}\) for every \(i,j\), where \(\delta_{ij}=1\) if \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. Equivalently, the mean vector is zero and the covariance matrix is the identity. Isotropy excludes measures supported on a proper affine subspace, so no lower-dimensional singular case is omitted by using a density. Locally Lipschitz means that every point has a neighborhood on which \(|f(y)-f(z)|\le L\|y-z\|_2\) for some finite \(L\); the neighborhood and constant may depend on the point. Such a function has a Euclidean derivative outside a Lebesgue-null set, and \(\nabla f\) is the vector of its partial derivatives there; set it to zero where the derivative does not exist. This choice on the null set does not affect integration against \(\mu\). Write \(\bar f=\int f\,d\mu\), which is finite by the second-moment assumption, and \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)=\int(f-\bar f)^2\,d\mu\). The gradient energy is the integral of \(\|\nabla f\|_2^2\). Define \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)\) as the infimum of all \(a\ge0\) for which the displayed inequality holds with \(a\) for every admissible function, with infimum of the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). The question asks whether these constants are uniformly bounded; it does not ask for their optimal universal value. No symmetry, product structure, differentiability of \(V\), bounded support or positive lower bound on its curvature is assumed. Uniform laws on full-dimensional convex bodies are included after isotropic normalization; a convex body is a compact convex set with nonempty interior. The problem is an analytic existence statement, with no oracle, encoding or algorithmic-time requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal Poincaré inequality with some finite real \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\), there exist an integer \(n\ge1\), a measure \(\mu\) satisfying all stated log-concavity and isotropy conditions, and an admissible locally Lipschitz \(f\) of finite second moment and finite gradient energy such that \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)>C\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu\). The dimension, measure and function may depend on \(C\). A single violation for one proposed numerical constant does not refute existence of some larger universal constant. A dimension-dependent bound, or a theorem restricted to linear, radial or quadratic functions or a narrower class of measures, is insufficient unless the proof also establishes the entire stated target. No optimal value of \(C\) is required. An equivalent geometric statement can qualify only with a Lean-checked implication proving this proposition or its negation; cited but unproved conjectural dependencies do not complete acceptance.
cards.status_note: The complete all-function KLS conjecture is explicitly open in Letwin’s 27 July 2026 preprint and Zhang’s 5 September 2026 sampling revision. The latter retains dependence on the KLS constant; its claimed mixing theorem does not resolve KLS. Live revision checks and bounded later-work searches on 14 September found no primary full resolution. Thin-shell and quadratic-form results are separately scoped. The new July and September proofs were not independently verified; source statements, conventions and implication directions were checked.

cards.title: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair conjecture
cards.formal: For every fixed finite simple graph H, is there a finite constant \(C_{H}\ge 1\) such that, for every finite connected simple undirected H-minor-free graph G with strictly positive real edge lengths, its shortest-path metric \(d_{G}\) admits a map \(f:V(G)\to \mathbb{R} ^{m}\) into some finite-dimensional \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) space satisfying \(d_{G}(u,v)\le \Vert f(u)- f(v)\Vert _{1}\le C_{H} d_{G}(u,v)\) for all vertices u,v?
cards.definitions: H-minor-free means that deleting vertices and edges and contracting edges of G cannot produce a graph isomorphic to H, after removing loops and duplicate edges. The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths, and \(d_{G}(u,v)\) is the minimum path length. In \(\mathbb{R} ^{m}, \Vert x- y\Vert _{1}=\sum_{j=1}^{m} |x_{j}- y_{j}|\). The displayed inequalities normalize the embedding to be noncontracting; permitting a common scaling factor gives the same distortion notion. The constant \(C_{H}\) may depend on the excluded graph H, but must be independent of |\(V(G)|\), the edge lengths and their ratio. The target dimension m and the map f may depend on the entire weighted graph and have no computational or dimension bound. This is an existence question for all vertex pairs simultaneously. It concerns undirected shortest-path distances themselves, without a snowflake transformation, average-pair guarantee or restriction to selected terminals.
