cards.title: Unknot recognition in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing algorithm and a constant c such that, on every explicit combinatorial knot diagram D of encoding length N, the algorithm decides in \(O((N+1)^{c})\) bit operations whether the represented knot in the 3-sphere is ambient isotopic to the unknot?
cards.definitions: A knot is a tame embedding of one circle into \(S^{3}\); the unknot is the isotopy class of a round circle. Ambient isotopy means a continuous family of homeomorphisms of \(S^{3}\) starting at the identity and carrying one embedded circle to the other at its endpoint. A diagram is a generic projection with transverse double crossings and specified over/under information. Encode it by an explicitly listed connected 4-regular planar multigraph, including loops when needed, its cyclic orders of half-edges at vertices, a distinguished outer face and the overpassing pair of opposite half-edges at each crossing. Tracing the opposite pairs must give one component. A separate constant-size encoding represents the crossing-free circle. The embedding is required to be a valid sphere embedding; malformed encodings may be rejected by polynomial-time combinatorial checks. If the diagram has n crossings, a standard such encoding has \(O(n \log (n+1))\) bits. The complexity parameter is the supplied encoding length N, not the minimum crossing number among equivalent diagrams. The input is explicit rather than a compressed description of an exponentially larger diagram. No disk, simplification sequence, knot invariant, auxiliary advice or promise of triviality is supplied. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

cards.title: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(C>0\) and \(k\ge 1\) exist such that every nonempty pointed d-dimensional convex polyhedron with n facets has vertex-edge graph diameter at most \(C(n+d)^{k}\)?
cards.definitions: A polyhedron is an intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces over the real numbers. Work in its affine hull, identified with \(R^{d}\), where \(d\ge 1\), and require it to be pointed, meaning that it contains no affine line; this ensures that its vertices are present. Both bounded polyhedra, called polytopes, and unbounded pointed polyhedra are included. The number n counts distinct facets in an irredundant description, rather than repeated input inequalities. The graph \(G(\mathrm{P})\) has one vertex per geometric vertex of P and an undirected edge between u and v precisely when their segment is a bounded one-dimensional face of P. An unbounded ray is not an extra graph vertex or an edge to infinity. Graph distance counts edges, each at unit cost; diameter is the maximum distance between vertices and is zero for a one-vertex polyhedron. The constants C,k must be independent of dimension, facet count, coordinates, coefficient bit length and the choice of polyhedron. Real coordinates are allowed, and no simplicity or nondegeneracy assumption is made. Paths need not improve any objective function, and no algorithm for finding them is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.status_note: No polynomial upper bound or superpolynomial counterexample for the stated worst-case edge-diameter problem was found through 11 September 2026. Natura’s 2026 result resolves the circuit analogue and explicitly leaves the combinatorial problem open. The card includes bounded and pointed unbounded polyhedra, counts facets, and imposes neither monotonicity nor an efficient path-finding requirement.

cards.title: Planar k-set extremal function
cards.formal: Let \(K_{2}(n,k)\) be the maximum, over sets P of n distinct points in $\mathbb R^2$ with no three collinear, of the number of distinct subsets \(S\subseteq \mathrm{P}\) of size k strictly separable from \(P\setminus S\) by a line. Determine \(K_{2}(n,k)\) up to universal constant factors, uniformly for all integers \(n\ge 2\) and \(1\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\).
cards.definitions: Strict separation means that there are real a,b,c with \((a,b)\ne (0,0), ax\)+by<c for every \((x,y)\in S\), and ax+by>c for every \((x,y)\in\)\(P\setminus S\). The objects counted are subsets S, not their infinitely many possible separating lines. Coordinates have no bounded-precision, grid, or random-distribution promise. The target is worst-case combinatorial complexity, not the running time of an enumeration algorithm. A matching bound means an asymptotic expression \(F(n,k)\) and absolute constants \(0<c_{0}\le C_{0}<\infty\) such that \(c_{0}F(n,k)\le K_{2}(n,k)\le C_{0}F(n,k)\) throughout the stated range, apart from finitely many n which can be absorbed into the constants. Bounds must cover k that grows with n. Complementation supplies the remaining values \(n/2<k<n; k=0,n\) each have one subset. This card specializes the original all-dimensions problem to the plane.
cards.answer_criterion: Determine a positive function \(F(n,k)\) and universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) with \(cF(n,k)\le K_{2}(n,k)\le CF(n,k)\) throughout \(n\ge 2\) and \(1\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\). Prove the universal upper bound and existence of matching point sets for every parameter pair in Lean. No predetermined formula grammar or closed form is required; a mere restatement of the defining extremum is insufficient. This asymptotic-complexity target uses constant-factor precision, not additive 0.01. A fixed-k result or the halving case alone does not determine the whole function.

cards.title: Linear-size sample compression
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant C such that every nonempty binary concept class \(H\subseteq \{0,1\}^{X}\) of finite VC dimension \(d\ge 1\) admits a labeled sample compression scheme with kernel bound k and side-information bound b satisfying \(k+b\le Cd\), in the model below? The same compressor and reconstructor must work for every finite H-realizable sample, independently of its size.
cards.definitions: The domain X is an arbitrary set, and a concept \(h\in H\) is a total function \(X\to \{0,1\}\). A finite set \(A\subseteq X\) is shattered if \(\{h|_{A}:h\in H\}=\{0,1\}^{A}; d\) is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A realizable sample is a finite set \(S\subseteq X\times \{0,1\}\) agreeing with some \(h\in H\). A scheme consists of deterministic maps \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\), which may depend on H, and nonnegative integers k,b. For every realizable \(S, \kappa (S)=(T,z)\), where \(T\subseteq S\) is an unordered labeled subset with |\(T|\le k\) and \(z\in \{0,1\}^{b}\). The reconstructor receives only T and z and produces a total predictor \(\rho (T,z):X\to \{0,1\}\) agreeing with every pair in S. It does not receive S, its size, the omitted points, or their indices. The side string has fixed length b; padding shorter strings changes only constant-factor size conventions. Reconstruction need not lie in H, be stable under deleting unused examples, or have any prescribed computational complexity. No probability distribution, efficiency, or measurability condition is part of this combinatorial existence question. Dimension zero is harmless: a nonempty such class has one labeling and needs no stored examples.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

cards.title: Learning parity with noise in polynomial time
cards.formal: For every fixed rational noise rate \(\eta\) with \(0<\eta <1/2\), does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every n and every secret \(s\in \{0,1\}^{n}\), recovers s with probability at least \(2/3\) from independent samples \((a,\langle a,s\rangle \oplus e)\), where a is uniform in \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and e is independently \(Bernoulli(\eta )\)?
cards.definitions: The inner product \(\langle a,s\rangle\) is \(\sum_{i} a_{i} s_{i}\) modulo two, and ⊕ is addition modulo two. The unknown s is fixed throughout an execution. Each requested sample uses a fresh independent uniform vector a and an independent error bit e, with \(\Pr [e=1]=\eta\). The learner knows n and the fixed rate \(\eta\), and receives only classical samples. It cannot choose a, request a noiseless label, identify which labels were corrupted, or make coherent quantum queries. For each fixed \(\eta\) the algorithm and its polynomial bound \(p\eta\) may depend on \(\eta\), but they must be uniform in n, without advice. Every execution uses at most \(p\eta (n)\) bit operations and requests at most \(p\eta (n)\) samples; reading and storing samples is charged. Polynomially many stored bits and repeated access to stored samples are allowed. The success probability is over the example generator and the learner’s random coins, for each fixed s. The desired output is the entire secret vector, not merely a predictor with unspecified advantage. No sparsity promise is imposed on s or on a. The quantifier over fixed rational \(\eta\) does not demand a running-time bound uniform as \(\eta\) approaches \(1/2\) with n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

cards.title: Learning Boolean juntas from uniform random examples
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that learns every Boolean k-junta on n variables from independent uniform random labelled examples in time polynomial in \(n, 2^{k}\) and \(1/\varepsilon\), with uniform-distribution error at most \(\varepsilon\) and success probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: For integers \(0\le k\le n, a k\)-junta is a function \(f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\) for which there is an unknown set \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,n\}, |S|\le k\), and an arbitrary Boolean function g on |S| bits such that \(f(x)=g\)(x restricted to S). The learner receives n,k and a positive integer \(t\ge 3\), setting \(\varepsilon =1/t\). Each requested example consists of an independently uniform \(x\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) and its exact, noiseless label \(f(x)\). The learner may request further independent examples, but cannot choose inputs to be labelled or obtain correlated examples. The output is a finite Boolean circuit h on n input bits; it need not itself be a k-junta. With probability at least \(2/3\) over all examples and internal random bits, Pr over a fresh uniform x that \(h(x)\ne f(x)\) is at most \(1/t\). One fixed classical probabilistic Turing machine must run, on every sample and random tape, for at most \((n+2^{k}+t)^{C}\) steps, up to a fixed multiplicative constant, for a universal constant C independent of n,k,t,f. Reading examples, computation and writing the circuit count toward this bound. Restricting \(\varepsilon\) to reciprocal integers is equivalent, up to polynomial factors, to the usual arbitrary-accuracy requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.status_note: No general learner with the stated polynomial dependence, or impossibility theorem for unrestricted learners, was found through 11 September 2026. Current sources retain the uniform-example barrier. Efficient membership-query, monotone-junta and correlated-random-walk results do not meet this exact model.

cards.title: Polynomial-time distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
cards.formal: Is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every \(n,s\ge 1\), every Boolean function f representable by a DNF with at most s terms on n variables, every distribution D on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\), and all accuracy and confidence parameters \(\varepsilon ,\delta \in (0,1)\), PAC learns f from independent D-distributed labelled examples in time polynomial in \(n,s,1/\varepsilon\) and \(\log (1/\delta )\)? The output may be any efficiently evaluable Boolean hypothesis; membership queries are not allowed.
cards.definitions: A literal is a variable \(x_{i}\) or its negation. A term is a conjunction of literals, and a disjunctive normal form \((\mathrm{DNF})\) is an OR of terms. Terms may have arbitrary width up to n after simplification. The size parameter s bounds the number of terms; counting literal occurrences instead changes polynomial bounds by at most a factor n. The target DNF is unknown: the learner is supplied only n, the upper bound s, and learning parameters. For an exact encoding, supply integers \(t,b\ge 2\) and set \(\varepsilon =1/t\) and \(\delta =2^{- b}\). One fixed probabilistic Turing machine must use at most \(p(n,s,t,b)\) steps for one fixed polynomial p, on every sequence of sample and random outcomes. Each example-oracle request supplies a fresh pair \((x,f(x))\) with x drawn independently from the same arbitrary unknown D; the learner cannot select x. Receiving and reading the n-bit sample counts toward the time bound. Samples are noiseless and realizable by the promised target. The output is an explicitly written deterministic Boolean circuit h on n input bits, not necessarily a DNF. With probability at least \(1- \delta\) over the examples and internal randomness, \(\Pr_{x\text{ drawn from }D}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon\). Writing and evaluating this circuit have polynomial cost. Reciprocal-integer accuracy and dyadic confidence suffice for the usual general parameters by rounding toward stronger guarantees. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.title: Distribution-free learning of two margin halfspaces
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized learner and one polynomial \(p\) with the following guarantee? For every dimension \(d\geq 1\), every \(0<\gamma,\varepsilon<1\), and every distribution \(D\) satisfying the realizability and margin promises below, the learner receives independent labeled examples from \(D\) and, within \(p(d,\lceil1/\gamma\rceil,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil)\) operations, outputs a hypothesis \(h\) such that \[\Pr_{\text{samples, learner}}\!\left[\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[h(x)\ne y]\leq\varepsilon\right]\geq 2/3.\] The hypothesis may be improper, but its evaluation on a new point must also take polynomial time in these parameters. No factorization or other restriction on the example distribution is imposed beyond the stated promises.
cards.definitions: The instance distribution is a Borel probability distribution on \(\mathbb R^{d}\times\{-1,+1\}\). There exist unknown unit vectors \(u,v\in\mathbb R^{d}\) and thresholds \(a,b\in\mathbb R\) such that, almost surely, \(\|x\|_{2}\leq1\), \(|\langle u,x\rangle+a|\geq\gamma\), \(|\langle v,x\rangle+b|\geq\gamma\), and \(y=+1\) precisely when both \(\langle u,x\rangle+a\geq0\) and \(\langle v,x\rangle+b\geq0\). In particular the margin promise applies to both defining hyperplanes, including on negatively labeled examples. The learner receives \(d,\gamma,\varepsilon\) and a sample oracle for independent draws from \(D\); it does not receive the unknown vectors, thresholds, a description of \(D\), membership queries or statistical-query oracles. Time is measured in the real-arithmetic model for the continuous-example formulation: a finite uniform program, with rational constants, exact real registers, integer indexing, arithmetic \(+, -, \times, /\) (division only by nonzero values), comparisons and independent fair random bits. Each arithmetic operation, comparison, register access and random bit costs one step; obtaining and reading a sample costs \(d+1\) steps. No operation extracts arbitrarily many bits of a real number in one step. The learner outputs a finite description of a deterministic prediction program together with finitely many stored real parameters; description length, storage, sample count, training time and evaluation time must obey fixed polynomial bounds. All bounds are worst-case over samples and internal randomness; only the accuracy guarantee is probabilistic. This explicitly fixes the arithmetic-cost convention for the source model, rather than asserting a finite-bit running-time theorem for arbitrary-precision real inputs.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified learner-existence statement or its negation in the specified arithmetic and sampling model. A positive answer includes the learner, its hypothesis representation, the polynomial training and evaluation bounds, and its distribution-independent accuracy guarantee. A negative answer must be unconditional for this model; hardness restricted to proper learners, statistical-query learners, a growing number of halfspaces, or an additional complexity assumption does not refute the statement.

cards.title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical cryptographic one-way function imply the existence of a classical public-key encryption scheme for one-bit messages, with negligible correctness error and security against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time chosen-plaintext adversary, in the plain model specified below? This is an unrelativized existence implication. The construction and its security proof may inspect the program of the one-way function and need not be black-box.
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is \(\lambda\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\), supplied as the unary string \(1^{\lambda}\). All algorithms are uniform classical Turing machines on bits: one finite program works for every parameter, with no advice, oracle or quantum resource. A PPT algorithm uses independent fair random bits and halts within a fixed polynomial in its total input length on every input and every random tape. Each algorithm has its own polynomial bound. Reading, computing, random-bit generation, communication and output all have ordinary bit-machine costs. Bit-string tuples use the component encoding \(s\mapsto1^{|s|}0s\); finite lists prepend an encoded binary component count. Binary integers have no leading zeros except the representation of zero. Explicitly proved polynomial-time equivalent encodings are acceptable.

A function \(\nu:\mathbb N_{\geq1}\to[0,1]\) is negligible if \(\forall d\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\;\exists\lambda_0\;\forall\lambda\geq\lambda_0:\nu(\lambda)\leq\lambda^{-d}\). A one-way function is a total deterministic polynomial-time map \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(I\),
\[\Pr[\,|Y|=\lambda\ \land\ f(Y)=f(X)\,]\]
is negligible, where \(X\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) and \(Y=I(1^{\lambda},f(X))\). The probability also includes the independent coins of \(I\). Any preimage of length \(\lambda\) counts as success; failure or a different output length does not. Injectivity and preservation of length are not required.

A candidate encryption scheme is a triple \((\mathsf{Gen},\mathsf{Enc},\mathsf{Dec})\) of uniform polynomial-time algorithms. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\) returns two finite bit strings \((pk,sk)\), the public and secret keys. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b)\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\), returns a finite ciphertext bit string \(c\). The deterministic algorithm \(\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,c)\) returns \(0\), \(1\), or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Algorithms are total on well-formed inputs, including arbitrary key and ciphertext strings; malformed encodings return a fixed failure response in polynomial time. Their runtime bounds use the full input length, so all honestly generated keys and ciphertexts have length polynomial in \(\lambda\). Encryption uses fresh private coins on each invocation, independently of key generation.

Correctness requires, for each \(b\in\{0,1\}\), negligible
\[\Pr[\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b))\ne b],\qquad (pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda}),\]
over key-generation and encryption coins; failure counts as an error. This is average correctness over honestly generated keys and coins, not a requirement that every key and every random tape decrypt correctly.

Security requires that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(E\) outputting a bit, its advantage
\[\left|\Pr[E(1^{\lambda},pk,c)=B]-\frac12\right|\]
be negligible, where \((pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\), \(B\) is an independent uniform bit, and \(c\leftarrow\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,B)\). All coins, including those of \(E\), are independent except for the displayed dependencies. The programs are public. The adversary may perform any polynomial amount of computation and generate encryptions of arbitrarily chosen bits using \(pk\) and its own fresh coins; it has no decryption oracle. This is the standard one-bit indistinguishability formulation of chosen-plaintext security for public-key encryption. Security holds for every such adversary, with its own negligible bound eventually at all sufficiently large parameters. There is no restriction to infinitely many parameters, to an average choice of the adversary, or to a particular fixed polynomial attack time.

There is no pre-existing shared secret, trusted setup, random oracle, auxiliary hardness assumption or quantum information. The quantifier order is: if some \(f\) satisfying the stated one-wayness condition exists, then some single scheme satisfying the format, cost, correctness and security requirements exists. Neither its algorithms nor its proof must use \(f\) through an oracle interface. A uniform compiler taking the code of \(f\) as input is not an additional requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this existence implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must obtain the stated uniform classical encryption scheme from the existence of one-way functions alone and prove the full correctness and chosen-plaintext guarantees. A negative answer must prove that a one-way function exists while no scheme in the stated class meets both guarantees. An oracle separation, a lower bound on a restricted class of reductions, a break of one proposed scheme, or a construction requiring some additional unproved hardness assumption does not settle the target. One-bit messages are the specified target; polynomially many independently encrypted bits yield the standard extension to longer messages with polynomial security loss. A cited or unchecked proof claim does not satisfy Lean acceptance.

cards.title: One-way functions from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal: Does \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) imply that there exists a deterministic polynomial-time computable function \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every constant \(c>0\), all sufficiently large n satisfy $\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,I}[\,|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)\,]\le n^{-c}$, where $z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x))$?
cards.definitions: \(U_{n}\) is the uniform distribution on n-bit strings. The function f is computed by one deterministic Turing machine in worst-case polynomial time; in particular its output length is polynomially bounded in n. The inverter receives n in unary and the output \(f(x)\), uses independent unbiased random bits, and runs in worst-case polynomial time in the length of its input on every random tape. Its output may be an n-bit candidate or failure. Finding any n-bit preimage counts as success, not only recovering the original x. The probability includes both the choice of x and the inverter’s coins. Formally, for every fixed inverter I and real \(c>0\) there exists \(N(I,c)\) such that the inequality holds for every \(n\ge N(I,c)\). This is eventual negligible inversion probability, not security only at infinitely many lengths. Algorithms have no oracle, nonuniform advice, trapdoor, or quantum computation. The premise \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) concerns ordinary uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision versus polynomial-time verification. The task is an existence implication and does not require a black-box construction or a particular proof method.

cards.title: Circuit obfuscation from polynomial-hard LWE
cards.formal: Does the decisional LWE assumption with the fixed polynomial parameters below imply the existence of indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no additional hardness, leakage-resilience, or circular-security assumption? The target is a classical polynomial-time obfuscator secure against classical polynomial-size adversaries.
cards.definitions: Fix \(q(n)\) to be the least prime at least \(n^{4}\) for every integer \(n\ge 2\). Let \(\chi _{n}\) be the discrete Gaussian on Z with probability of e proportional to \(\exp (- \pi e^{2}/n^{2})\). The assumed LWE statement is: for every polynomial \(m(n)\), the ensembles (\(A,A s+e\) mod q) and \((A,u)\) are computationally indistinguishable, where A is uniform in \(Z_{q}^{m\times n}, s\) is uniform in \(Z_{q}^{n}\), the m coordinates of e are independent \(\chi _{n}\) samples, and u is independent uniform in \(Z_{q}^{m}\). Indistinguishable means every polynomial-size classical circuit family has negligible advantage in n; negligible means smaller than \(n^{- c}\) eventually for every constant \(c>0\). No secret-dependent leakage is supplied. An obfuscator O is a uniform probabilistic algorithm running in time polynomial in \(\lambda +|C|\) that outputs a Boolean circuit \(O(1^{\lambda},C)\) of polynomial size. Circuits are finite acyclic \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) circuits with fan-in at most two, a specified list of input and output bits, and explicit binary descriptions; |C| is description length. For every polynomial p, there is negligible \(\mu _{p}\) such that for every |\(C|\le p(\lambda )\), with probability at least \(1- \mu _{p}(\lambda )\) over the obfuscator’s coins the output circuit agrees with C on ALL inputs. For every pair of circuit sequences \(C_{0},\lambda\) and \(C_{1},\lambda\) with polynomially bounded, equal description lengths, the same input/output lengths and identical functions, their obfuscations are computationally indistinguishable against all polynomial-size circuit families. Both functionality and security quantify over all such circuits, without requiring an efficiently checkable proof of equivalence. There is no oracle, trusted setup, quantum state, or restriction to a special circuit family. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.title: Unleveled fully homomorphic encryption from LWE alone
cards.formal: Does ordinary polynomial-modulus decisional LWE, with the parameter convention below, imply a classical compact fully homomorphic encryption scheme whose keys are generated without an evaluation-depth bound, secure against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries without any additional circular-security or key-dependent-message assumption?
cards.definitions: Fix the following ordinary LWE assumption: for every fixed integer \(c\ge 3\) and polynomial sample count \(M(d)\), let \(q(d)\) be the least prime at least \(d^{c}\), let s be uniform in \(Z_{q}^{d}\), let A be uniform in \(Z_{q}^{M(d)\times d}\), and let the coordinates of e be independent integers with probability proportional to \(\exp (- \pi z^{2}/(4d))\), reduced modulo q. The ensembles (A,As+e mod q) and \((A,u)\), for independent uniform \(u\in Z_{q}^{M(d)}\), are computationally indistinguishable against nonuniform classical circuits of size polynomial in d. Thus the error distribution is the discrete Gaussian \(D_{Z,2\sqrt{d}}\); only ordinary independently generated LWE samples are assumed hard. The FHE scheme has uniform classical polynomial-time algorithms \(Gen(1^{\lambda})\to\)(pk,evk,sk), \(Enc(pk,b)\), Eval(evk,\(C,c_{1},\ldots ,c_{t}\)), and \(Dec(sk,c)\), with bit plaintexts and Boolean circuits over AND, OR and NOT. Gen takes no circuit-size or depth bound. There is one fixed polynomial P such that keys, fresh bit ciphertexts, evaluated one-bit ciphertexts and the time to decrypt a valid output are bounded by \(\mathrm{P}(\lambda )\), independently of C and t. Evaluation is polynomial-time in \(\lambda\) and its total input length. For every polynomial p, uniformly over all circuits C of size and input count at most \(p(\lambda )\) and all input bits \(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{t}\), decrypting Eval on independent encryptions of these bits equals \(C(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{t})\), except with negligible probability over generation, encryption and evaluation. Ordinary decryption is correct with negligible error. Given both pk and evk, every nonuniform polynomial-size classical adversary has negligible advantage in distinguishing an encryption of 0 from one of 1. Negligible means smaller than \(\lambda ^{-a}\) eventually for every \(a>0\). No subsequent secret-key assistance, ideal oracle, external trusted setup, superpolynomial adversary-hardness assumption, functional-encryption assumption or obfuscation assumption is allowed. This fixes a polynomial-modulus version of “standard LWE”; it does not assume any encryptions of secrets or correlated hints are secure.

This card fixes polynomial-modulus LWE, nonuniform classical security and fresh-input FHE correctness.

cards.title: Sub-square-root share-size exponents in perfect secret sharing
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants \(K>0\) and \(0<c<1/2\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\) and every monotone access structure \(\Gamma\) on \([n]\) with \(\varnothing \notin \Gamma\) and \([n]\in \Gamma\), there exists a perfect secret-sharing scheme for a uniform one-bit secret with \(\max _{i} \log _{2}|S_{i}|\le K\cdot 2^{cn}\), where \(S_{i}\) is the finite alphabet of participant i’s share?
cards.definitions: \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). An access structure \(\Gamma \subseteq 2^{[n]}\) is monotone when \(A\in \Gamma\) and \(A\subseteq B\subseteq [n]\) imply \(B\in \Gamma\). A scheme is a joint probability distribution of a secret B uniform on \(\{0,1\}\) and shares \(X_{i}\in S_{i}\), where each \(S_{i}\) is a finite nonempty set. For each \(A\in \Gamma\) there is a deterministic map \(r_{A}:\prod _{i\in A}S_{i}\to \{0,1\}\) such that \(r_{A}((X_{i})_{i\in A})=B\) with probability one. For each \(A\notin \Gamma\), the conditional distributions of \((X_{i})_{i\in A}\) given \(B=0\) and \(B=1\) are identical. This is exact reconstruction and perfect information-theoretic privacy, with arbitrary collusion within A. Share size is the base-two logarithm of its alphabet cardinality, not its Shannon entropy or the sum over participants. It is normalized by the secret size of one bit. There is no linearity, field, threshold, computation-time or uniform construction requirement. The scheme may depend on the whole finite access structure. K,c must be universal. Rounding \(\log _{2}|S_{i}|\) up to an integer encoding length changes K only by an absolute factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some universal \(K>0\) and \(0<c<1/2\) satisfy the stated worst-share bound for every permitted access structure, or prove the logical negation in Lean. A negative answer must show that for every such \(K,c\) some access structure admits no perfect scheme with that bound, allowing all finite share alphabets and all joint distributions in the definition. The object quantified over is a general scheme; it need not be linear or efficiently constructed.
cards.status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. Nir’s August 2026 ECCC report, Theorem 1.5, claims a general scheme with maximal share size \(2^{0.496n+o(n)}\), directly implying the stated strict threshold after adjustment of the universal constant. The target and theorem were compared; the proof was not independently verified. This remains an uncertain claimed resolution.

cards.title: Quantum PCP conjecture
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(k,d\ge 1\) and a rational constant \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\) such that the following promise problem is QMA-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Input is a list of \(m\le (n+1)^{d} k\)-local Hermitian terms \(H_{i}\) on \(n\ge 1\) qubits and rational \(a<b\) in \([0,1]\), with \(0\preceq H_{i}\preceq I\) and \(b- a\ge \varepsilon\). For \(H=(1/m)\sum_{i} H_{i}\), distinguish \(\lambda _{\mathrm{min}}(H)\le a\) from \(\lambda _{\mathrm{min}}(H)\ge b\).
cards.definitions: Here \(1\le m\); each term is specified by at most k distinct qubit indices and the complete matrix on those qubits, with rational real and imaginary parts encoded by signed binary numerators and positive denominators. It is tensored with identity on the other qubits. n is written in unary, thresholds in binary rational notation; N counts every supplied bit. \(\lambda _{\mathrm{min}}\) is the smallest eigenvalue. \(M\preceq N\) means that \(N- M\) is positive semidefinite, equivalently \(z*(N- M)z\ge 0\) for every complex vector z. Inputs violating the matrix promises or with \(a<\lambda _{\mathrm{min}}(H)<b\) are outside the promise. QMA consists of disjoint pairs \((Y,N_{0})\) of sets of binary strings with a polynomial-time uniform quantum verifier: on x it uses polynomially many qubits and gates over {H,T,CNOT}, an arbitrary polynomial-qubit witness, and auxiliary qubits initialized to |\(0\rangle\). \(H=2^{- 1/2}((1,1),(1,- 1))\) is the Hadamard matrix, \(T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\), and CNOT flips its target when its control is 1. A designated final qubit is measured. For \(x\in Y\) some witness gives acceptance probability \(\ge 2/3\); for \(x\in N_{0}\) every witness gives probability \(\le 1/3\). A deterministic machine produces the verifier circuit from x in polynomial time. QMA-hard means that for every such pair there is a deterministic polynomial-time map sending Y into the low-energy case and \(N_{0}\) into the high-energy case, always producing legal instances on promised inputs. Constants \(k,d,\varepsilon\) are shared by the target problem; reduction polynomials may depend on the source promise problem.

cards.title: BPP versus BQP
cards.formal: Is $\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}$? Equivalently, is there a total decision language \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* with a uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm that is correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input, but no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time classical algorithm with the same per-input correctness guarantee?
cards.definitions: BPP uses a single classical probabilistic Turing machine with independent unbiased coins, worst-case time \(C(n+1)^{k}\) on n-bit inputs, and error probability at most \(1/3\) separately for every input. BQP uses a polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size quantum circuits: a deterministic classical machine on \(1^{n}\) generates the circuit description in polynomial time. Fix gates H, T, and CNOT, where H is the Hadamard gate, \(T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\), and CNOT is controlled bit-flip. Gates may act on any addressed qubits. The input register starts in |\(x\rangle\), polynomially many auxiliary qubits start in |\(0\rangle\), and one designated qubit is measured in the computational basis at the end. Its output must equal the membership bit with probability at least \(2/3\) for every x. The family has no advice, oracle gates, postselection, or arbitrary real-number gate parameters. Size and register bounds use fixed polynomial exponents independent of n. Equivalent standard uniform quantum-machine definitions give the same class. The problem concerns one-bit decisions on all binary strings, with no promise on the input. It does not ask for exact amplitudes, full output distributions, or a separation restricted to shallow classical circuits.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.status_note: Wigderson’s Conjecture 11.4 explicitly asks for strict containment. Primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no unrelativized separation of these bounded-error decision classes was located. Oracle and shallow-circuit sampling advantages are recorded with their model restrictions.

cards.title: Area law for gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians
cards.formal: For every fixed local dimension \(q\ge 2\), interaction range \(r\ge 1\), interaction incidence bound \(g\ge 1\), norm bound \(J>0\), and spectral gap \(\Delta >0\), is there a finite constant \(C=C(q,r,g,J,\Delta )\) such that every Hamiltonian H described below, on every square lattice \(\Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\), has unique ground state \(\psi\) satisfying \(S(\rho _{A})\le C|\partial A|\) for every \(A\subseteq \Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\)?
cards.definitions: Let \(\mathrm{L}\ge 1\) be an integer, \(\Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}=\{1,\ldots ,\mathrm{L}\}^{2}\) with open boundaries, and the Hilbert space be the tensor product of \(C^{q}\) over its sites. Write \(H=\sum_{a} h_{a}\), where each \(h_{a}\) is Hermitian and acts only on a nonempty support \(X_{a}\subseteq \Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\) of diameter at most r in the maximum-coordinate metric. Each site belongs to at most g supports, counting terms with the same support separately, and the operator norm of every \(h_{a}\) is at most J. Suppose H has a unique normalized lowest-energy eigenvector \(\psi\) and its next eigenvalue is at least \(\Delta\) above the lowest eigenvalue. This is a gap of the entire Hamiltonian; no spectral-gap condition is imposed on subregions or subsets of terms. For \(A\subseteq \Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\), let \(A^{c}\) be its complement in \(\Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\) and \(\rho _{A}=Tr_{A^{c}}(|\psi \rangle \langle \psi |)\) and \(S(\rho _{A})=- Tr(\rho _{A} \log _{2} \rho _{A})\), with \(0 \log _{2} 0=0\). The boundary \(\partial A\) is the set of nearest-neighbor lattice edges with exactly one endpoint in A; its cardinality is the boundary length in lattice units. Empty and full regions have entropy zero. The local parameters and C must be independent of L, A, and the actual interaction matrices. Interactions may vary from site to site and with L. They need not commute or share a simultaneous minimum-energy state; translation invariance and frustration freeness are not assumed. No approximation or state-preparation algorithm is requested.

cards.title: Information-theoretic classical verification of quantum computation
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform interactive protocol \((\mathrm{P},V)\) for the following promise problem? Input is an explicit quantum circuit C over {H,T,CNOT}, starting on all-zero qubits, with one designated output bit and binary description length N. Let \(p(C)\) be the probability of output 1. YES instances have \(p(C)\ge 2/3\) and NO instances have \(p(C)\le 1/3\). V is a classical probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm and the honest P is a quantum polynomial-time algorithm; they exchange only classical messages. On every YES instance, Pr[V accepts after interacting with P]\(\ge 2/3\). On every NO instance, for every computationally unbounded cheating prover P*, Pr[V accepts after interacting with P*]\(\le 1/3\). Both honest running times, the number of rounds and total communication must be polynomial in N.
cards.definitions: H is the Hadamard gate, \(T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\), and CNOT is controlled NOT. The circuit explicitly specifies its qubits and gates, with at most N qubits. The promise excludes intermediate acceptance probabilities; no answer is required there. The two parties know C. The verifier may use private classical random coins, but has no trusted quantum memory, operations or measurements. The honest prover starts without an input-dependent advice state and uses a uniform polynomial-size quantum computation with classical control. All communication is through a single classical interface to one prover. Soundness quantifies over arbitrary adaptive response strategies with no computational bound; probabilities include the verifier’s coins and any prover randomness or measurements. There is no trusted setup, shared secret, second noncommunicating prover or cryptographic assumption. Fixed constant completeness and soundness gaps are the target; no constant-round requirement is imposed. This circuit promise problem expresses verification for arbitrary BQP computations. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.title: NPT bound entanglement
cards.formal: Do there exist finite integers \(a,b\ge 2\) and a bipartite density matrix \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb{C} ^{a}\otimes \mathbb{C} ^{b}\) such that \(\rho\) has negative partial transpose, but \(\langle \psi |(\rho ^{\Gamma _{B}})^{\otimes k}|\psi \rangle \ge 0\) for every integer \(k\ge 1\) and every unit vector \(\psi\) of Schmidt rank at most two across \((\mathbb{C} ^{a})^{\otimes k}:(\mathbb{C} ^{b})^{\otimes k}\)?
cards.definitions: A density matrix is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix with trace one. In fixed local orthonormal bases, partial transpose on B is defined by \((\rho ^{\Gamma _{B}})_{ij,k\ell}=\rho _{i\ell ,kj}\). Negative partial transpose (NPT) means that \(\rho ^{\Gamma _{B}}\) has at least one negative eigenvalue; it does not mean that the whole matrix is negative semidefinite. Schmidt rank is the minimum number of product vectors whose sum is \(\psi\). Tensor powers represent independent copies of the same fixed state. A state is k-copy distillable exactly when a Schmidt-rank-at-most-two vector makes the displayed expectation strictly negative. Thus the proposed state is undistillable for every finite number of copies. Operationally, Alice and Bob may use arbitrary local quantum operations, local auxiliary systems and unlimited classical communication in both directions, but no quantum communication or additional shared entanglement. Distillability means that they can asymptotically obtain Bell pairs \((|00\rangle +|11\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\) at a positive rate with error tending to zero. The finite-copy criterion above is equivalent to positive distillability in this model.

cards.title: Martin’s conjecture
cards.formal: Assume \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\). Is the following conjunction true for all total Turing-invariant functions \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\)? Part I: every such \(f\) is constant in Turing degree on a cone or computes its input on a cone. Part II: the relation \(\leq_M\) of Turing reducibility on a cone prewellorders the set \(\mathcal F\) of all such functions above the identity on a cone, and for every \(f\in\mathcal F\), its pointwise Turing jump \(f'\) has rank exactly \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)+1\) in that same prewellorder. All functions, cones, ordinals and quantifiers are interpreted within the stated set-theoretic universe.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\omega=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) and \(2^{\omega}=\{x:\omega\to\{0,1\}\}\). Such a real is identified with the subset \(\{n:x(n)=1\}\) of \(\omega\). Fix an acceptable effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\omega}\) of ordinary oracle Turing programs with natural-number inputs and outputs. The oracle answers membership queries in a real. Define \(x\leq_T y\) to mean that some index \(e\) satisfies \(\Phi_e^y(n)\downarrow=x(n)\) for every \(n\in\omega\), with no time bound. The single index computes the entire real, and may depend on \(x,y\). Define \(x\equiv_T y\) by mutual reducibility. A Turing degree is an equivalence class for \(\equiv_T\). The jump \(y'\) is the characteristic real of \(\{e:\Phi_e^y(e)\text{ halts}\}\). Any acceptable effective numbering gives the same induced operation on degrees.

A total function \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\) is Turing-invariant when \(\forall x,y:\ x\equiv_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\). No computability, measurability, Borel definability, order preservation or uniform production of reduction indices is required. The quantifiers concern functions on reals with this invariance property; no choice of a representative from every Turing degree is assumed.

For \(a\in2^{\omega}\), the cone with base \(a\) is \(C_a=\{x\in2^{\omega}:a\leq_T x\}\). Being constant in degree on a cone means
\[\exists a,b\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\equiv_T b.\]
Being above the identity on a cone means
\[\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ x\leq_T f(x).\]
The base may depend on \(f\). Constancy is equality of degrees, not literal equality of output reals. A cone requirement holds for every real in that cone, not merely infinitely many reals or a set of full ordinary Lebesgue measure.

For invariant \(f,g\), define
\[f\leq_M g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\leq_T g(x).\]
The base may depend on both functions; no single base must work for all comparisons. Set \(f\equiv_M g\) when both \(f\leq_M g\) and \(g\leq_M f\). Let \(\mathrm{id}(x)=x\) and \(\mathcal F=\{f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}: f\text{ is Turing-invariant and }\mathrm{id}\leq_M f\}\). The prewellorder clause means that \(\leq_M\) is reflexive, transitive and total on \(\mathcal F\), and that the induced order on the set \(\mathcal F/{\equiv_M}\) is a well-order: every nonempty subset of that quotient has a least member. Its strict order is \([g]<[f]\) when \(g\leq_M f\) and \(f\not\leq_M g\). When this clause holds, \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)\) is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly below \([f]\), with its least class having rank zero. The pointwise jump is \(f'(x)=(f(x))'\). The \(+1\) in Part II is ordinal successor, and the rank is computed in the full quotient above the identity, not a selected definable subclass.

The background \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. Full dependent choice \(\mathsf{DC}\) asserts that for every nonempty set \(S\), every relation \(R\subseteq S\times S\) with \(\forall s\in S\;\exists t\in S:\ sRt\), and every \(s_0\in S\), there is a sequence \((s_n)_{n\in\omega}\) starting at \(s_0\) with \(s_nRs_{n+1}\) for all \(n\). The axiom of determinacy \(\mathsf{AD}\) asserts that for every set \(W\subseteq\omega^{\omega}\), the following perfect-information game is determined. Players I and II alternate choosing natural numbers, with I moving at even-numbered stages starting at zero; I wins exactly when the resulting sequence belongs to \(W\). A strategy assigns a next move to every finite history at that player’s turn, and is winning if every infinite play compatible with it is won by that player. Determined means that one player has such a winning strategy. No regularity condition is imposed on \(W\). These are internal set-theoretic axioms; the full axiom of choice is not added to them.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of both parts of the conjunction under \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\), or a refutation of at least one part under that same background. A refutation of Part I must establish the existence of an invariant function that is neither constant in degree on any cone nor above the identity on any cone. A refutation of Part II must establish failure of the stated full prewellorder or, when that prewellorder exists, failure of the exact jump-successor clause. A result only for uniformly invariant, Borel, regressive or order-preserving functions does not prove the full conjunction. Counterexamples obtained with the full axiom of choice do not refute the stated determinacy version. The Lean formalization must represent the set-theoretic background faithfully, for example through an internal set universe and its satisfaction relation, with all reals and functions interpreted there; importing ambient choice into that universe and deriving a contradiction with determinacy is not a proof of this target. No unproved classification or uniformity principle may be substituted for a required part.

cards.title: Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness versus Martin-Löf randomness
cards.formal: Is every Kolmogorov–Loveland random infinite binary sequence Martin-Löf random with respect to the fair-coin product measure?
cards.definitions: Work in Cantor space \(2^{N}\), with coordinates numbered \(0,1,\ldots\) and fair-coin product measure \(\mu\). For a finite binary string \(\sigma\), the cylinder \([\sigma ]\)={\(X:\sigma\) is a prefix of X} has measure \(2^{- |\sigma |}\). A Martin-Löf test is a sequence \((U_{k})_{k\ge 1}\) of open sets obtained by one algorithm enumerating pairs \((k,\sigma )\), with \(U_{k}\) equal to the union of its enumerated cylinders for index k and \(\mu (U_{k})\le 2^{- k}\). A sequence X is Martin-Löf random if for every such test \(X\notin \bigcap _{k} U_{k}\). A Kolmogorov–Loveland betting strategy starts with capital 1. From the finite history h of bits already revealed, a partial computable procedure outputs a previously unqueried coordinate j and a rational multiplier \(q\in [0,2]\), before seeing \(X(j)\). The selected coordinates can be reconstructed from the earlier history and the same procedure; no coordinate may be selected twice along any run. After \(X(j)\) is revealed, the capital is multiplied by q if the bit is 0 and by \(2- q\) if it is 1, and that bit is appended to h. Thus each bet preserves expected capital under a fresh unbiased bit and cannot create debt. \(q=1\) allows reading a bit without risking capital. The next coordinate may depend on all revealed values and need not exceed previous coordinates. If the procedure fails to produce its next action, no further capital is earned. There are no oracle, running-time or space allowances beyond ordinary partial computability. A strategy succeeds on X if its capital at completed bets has unbounded supremum. X is Kolmogorov–Loveland random if every such strategy has bounded capital on X; the bound may depend on both X and the strategy. Rational multipliers suffice for the standard notion, and allowing partial rather than total computable strategies does not change the resulting class.

cards.title: Superpolynomial Extended Frege lower bounds
cards.formal: Is classical Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every pair of integers \(C\ge1,c\ge1\), does there exist a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Extended Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\) has binary encoding length \(|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+2)^c\)? The formula and proof encodings and the fixed proof rules are specified below.
cards.definitions:
A propositional formula is a finite syntax tree built from variables \(v_i\), indexed by \(i\in\mathbb N\), unary negation and binary material implication. Its Boolean value under an assignment \(v_i\mapsto\{0,1\}\) is defined recursively, with \(A	o B\) false exactly when A is true and B is false. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. Let code(a), for \(a\ge0\), be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, with \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)floor+1\). Encode \(v_i\) as 00 followed by code(i), \(
eg A\) as 01 followed by the encoding of A, and \(A	o B\) as 10 followed by the encodings of A and B. This prefix syntax contains the whole formula tree, not a circuit or a program generating it; \(|\varphi|\) is its bit length. Fix the three classical Frege axiom schemes \(A	o(B	o A)\), \((A	o(B	o C))	o((A	o B)	o(A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o
eg A)	o(A	o B)\). An instance substitutes arbitrary formulas for A, B and C consistently. Modus ponens infers B from two earlier lines A and \(A	o B\). An extension introduction adds two consecutive lines \(e	o	heta\) and \(	heta	o e\), where e is a variable absent from the target formula, theta and every line before this pair. The defining formula theta may use variables of the target and previously introduced extension variables, so definitions are acyclic. Freshness is checked before the pair, not between its two lines. There are no unproved hypotheses. A proof is a finite nonempty list of lines justified by these axiom schemes, modus ponens or such an extension pair; its last line is exactly the target formula and contains no extension variables. Earlier lines can be cited any number of times. There is no depth bound, tree-like proof restriction or restriction on the sizes of intermediate formulas. For a complete proof encoding, first write code(m) for its number of lines, and then encode each line with a two-bit tag, its metadata and its entire formula in the prefix syntax above. Tag 00 stores the axiom-scheme number 1, 2 or 3 with code; tag 01 stores with code the two earlier, one-based line indices for modus ponens, in the order A then A implies B; tag 10 stores with code the index of the fresh extension variable and must be followed immediately by a tag-11 line giving the reverse implication for the same definition. Tag 11 has no metadata and is valid only as that second line of an extension pair. The first extension formula uniquely determines theta, and both implication formulas are fully written and counted. Missing or trailing bits and invalid justifications are rejected. The proof length counts all bits, including the line count, formulas, variable indices, rule tags and inference references. This is a fixed polynomial-time checkable presentation of classical EF, polynomially equivalent to the usual finite Frege bases with extension. EF is complete, so every tautology has some finite proof; the issue is a common polynomial bound. The chosen binary encoding and paired extension rule fix presentation details without changing polynomial boundedness. The hard formula may depend on C and c; no polynomial-time procedure generating a hard family is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed lower-bound assertion or its logical negation. The affirmative answer must, for every polynomial bound \(C(n+2)^c\), establish a tautology whose every valid EF proof exceeds that bound. The negative answer must establish fixed integers C,c for which every tautology has some valid EF proof of length at most \(C(|\varphi|+2)^c\); it need not give a polynomial-time proof-search algorithm. A bound for one search procedure, for bounded-depth or ordinary Frege, for a different logic, or for an algebraic encoding without a valid polynomial-size propositional translation does not settle this target.

The August 2026 preprint concerns different logics. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified classical EF resolution. The checked Pich–Santhanam version is the 2023 preprint, not its inaccessible journal version; the cited proofs have not been independently recertified.

cards.title: Frege versus Extended Frege
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C>0\) and \(k\ge 1\) such that every Extended Frege proof \(\pi\) of a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) has some ordinary Frege proof \(\rho\) of the same formula with |\(\rho |\le C(|\pi |+2)^{k}\)? Equivalently, if \(sF(\varphi )\) and \(sEF(\varphi )\) are the minimum proof sizes in the two systems, is \(sF(\varphi )\) polynomially bounded in \(sEF(\varphi )\), uniformly over all tautologies?
cards.definitions:
Fix formulas over negation \(
eg\) and material implication →, with binary-encoded variable indices. Ordinary Frege uses the axiom schemes \(A	o (B	o A), (A	o (B	o C))	o ((A	o B)	o (A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o 
eg A)	o (A	o B)\), and modus ponens: infer B from A and \(A	o B\). A proof is a finite sequence ending with \(\varphi\); earlier lines may be cited and reused without restriction. Extended Frege adds acyclic definitions, introducing the pair \(e	o 	heta\) and \(	heta 	o e\), where e is a new variable absent from \(\varphi , 	heta\) and all preceding lines. \(	heta\) may use variables of \(\varphi\) and earlier extension variables. The final formula contains no extension variables. Proof size is the complete binary encoding length of every explicitly written line, definition and inference reference. No formula-depth, proof-depth or tree-shape bound is imposed. These presentations are polynomially equivalent to the usual finite-basis Frege and Extended Frege systems. The target is existence of short translated proofs: it does not require a polynomial-time function that finds \(ho\) from \(\pi\). In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.title: Log-rank conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,k\ge1\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\), for arbitrary nonempty finite sets X and Y, satisfies \(D(f)\le C\bigl(\log_2(r(f)+2)\bigr)^k\)? Here r(f) is the rank over the real numbers of its zero-one communication matrix, and D(f) is its exact deterministic communication complexity in bits.
cards.definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\), Bob receives \(y\in Y\), and both know the complete function f, its finite domains and their chosen protocol. These shared data are not charged as communication. A protocol is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node specifies its sender and a function from that sender’s input set to \(\{0,1\}\). At that node the sender transmits this one bit, and both parties follow the corresponding edge; the node already records the preceding transcript. Every leaf is labeled 0 or 1. For every pair (x,y), the reached leaf must be labeled f(x,y), so both parties determine the exact answer. The cost is the maximum number of transmitted bits on any input pair, equivalently the tree depth after deleting unreachable branches. D(f) is the minimum cost among all correct trees; a finite protocol always exists. The protocol may depend arbitrarily on f, and its description length, local computation and number of communication rounds have no separate bound or charge. The communication matrix is \(M_f=(f(x,y))_{x\in X,y\in Y}\), treating its zeroes and ones as real scalars. Define \(r(f)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M_f)\), the dimension of its column span over \(\mathbb R\). The particular enumeration of either domain does not matter. Rank zero means the all-zero function, which has D(f)=0, and the all-one function also has D(f)=0. The term r+2 avoids a zero or undefined logarithm at small ranks without changing the asymptotic conjecture. The same C and k must work for every choice of domains and function; the protocol need not be generated uniformly from the table. The statement has no promise pairs, missing matrix entries, distribution on inputs, randomness, quantum messages, approximation or one-way restriction. Rank over a finite field, approximate rank and sign rank are not the parameter used here. Some sources encode outputs by minus one and plus one. With \(A=2M_f-J\), where J is the all-one matrix, the two ordinary real ranks differ by at most one and the output relabeling does not change D(f); with the r+2 convention these formulations have the same polynomial-boundedness question. The explicit negation is: for every pair of integers C,k at least one, there exist nonempty finite X,Y and a total f such that \(D(f)>C(\log_2(r(f)+2))^k\). No effective generator of the counterexample functions is added.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a single pair of universal constants C,k satisfying the displayed inequality, or prove its quantified negation excluding every such pair. An affirmative proof must apply to every total function in the exact interactive protocol model; it need not compute an optimal protocol efficiently. A negative proof must give arbitrarily strong failures of polynomial dependence on log-rank, with examples permitted to depend on C and k. Failure of one proposed exponent, a result for partial functions, or a bound using approximate rank, sign rank, randomness or quantum communication does not meet this target.
cards.status_note: The August 2026 equivalent-formulations paper explicitly states that the total deterministic log-rank conjecture remains unresolved, with the square-root-rank upper bound. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution. The new lifting proof and its comparison of suppressed logarithmic factors were not independently verified; fixed polynomial lower bounds and partition reformulations do not settle the universal conjecture.

cards.title: Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist a finite universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every Boolean function \(f:\{- 1,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,1\}, H(f)\le C I(f)\), where \(H(f)\) is the base-two Shannon entropy of its squared Fourier coefficients and \(I(f)\) is its total influence under the uniform distribution, as defined below?
cards.definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). For \(S\subseteq [n]\), let \(\chi _{S}(x)=\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}\), with \(\chi _{\varnothing}=1\), and let \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum _{x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}}f(x)\chi _{S}(x)\). Put \(q_{S}=\hat\{f\}(S)^{2}\); Parseval gives \(\sum _{S} q_{S}=1\). Define \(H(f)=\sum _{S} q_{S} \log _{2}(1/q_{S})\), with a zero summand when \(q_{S}=0\). If x is uniform and \(x^{\oplus i}\) differs only by flipping coordinate i, define \(I_{i}(f)=\Pr [f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})]\) and \(I(f)=\sum _{i=1}^{n} I_{i}(f)=\sum _{S} |S|q_{S}\). All Boolean functions are quantified, without circuit-size, monotonicity, balance, or efficient-computability assumptions. The same C must work for all dimensions and all functions. Constant functions have \(H(f)=I(f)=0\) and satisfy the non-strict inequality.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

cards.title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: For every real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(q\ge3\) such that no q-SAT decider A has a bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F, for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The width q may depend on epsilon but is fixed independently of the input. Equivalently, is \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\)? This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.definitions: Fix an integer clause-width bound \(q\ge 3\). A q-CNF formula is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most q literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\), with \(1\le i\le n\). The variables that occur are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so n counts distinct variables, not clauses or input bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment satisfies the formula if every clause has at least one true literal. An empty clause is false; the empty conjunction is true and has n=0. For a completely specified binary encoding, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), for a nonnegative integer a, be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). Encode n and the number m of clauses with this code, then each clause by its coded length followed by its literals. Each literal is a sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negated) and the code of its variable index. All indicated lists must be fully present, with no trailing bits, valid indices and every declared variable occurring. Let L be the complete bit length. Ill-formed strings, including clauses wider than q, are rejected. No density, satisfiability-count, occurrence or input-distribution promise is imposed. A q-SAT decider A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes only the cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The total transition count includes parsing, input access and all internal work. A must halt on all inputs, decide satisfiability exactly on valid q-CNF formulas, and reject malformed strings in polynomial time in their length. It receives no advice, random bits, quantum operations, oracle or precomputed instance information. The machine may depend on the fixed q. For a valid formula F, let \(t_A(F)\) be its runtime and \(n(F),L(F)\) its variable count and bit length. An exponent \(\alpha\ge 0\) is attainable at width q if there exist such a decider A and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) with \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F. The constants are independent of F. Define \(s_q\) as the infimum of all attainable exponents. This set is nonempty because exhaustive assignment testing gives an attainable exponent 1, so \(0\le s_q\le1\). The infimum need not itself be attainable. Polynomial factors in L remain explicit, including when clauses are repeated many times. The chosen explicit syntax and malformed-input normalization do not impose a new satisfiability promise; they fix the bit model for the source’s exponential-rate question. The sequence \(s_q\) is nondecreasing: a decider for width q+1 also decides the width-q restriction after checking its syntax. Since every \(s_q\le1\), its limit exists. The quantified statement says that no fixed positive saving from the exponent 1 works for all fixed widths. Its negation is that there exists one real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that for each integer \(q\ge3\) there are a q-SAT decider \(A_q\) and constants \(C_q,d_q\) with \(t_{A_q}(F)\le C_q2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_q}\) for every q-CNF formula F. The algorithm and polynomial factor may depend on q and the selected epsilon. There is no added requirement of one algorithm receiving q as an input, nor of an effective procedure generating \(A_q\) from q. Each individual machine is uniform over its formula inputs. Infima need not be attained; the equivalence uses the available slack between a limit below 1 and 1.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed deterministic all-width proposition, equivalently a proof that \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\) or that this limit is strictly below 1. A refutation must establish one positive exponential saving valid at every fixed width, with the algorithm and polynomial factors allowed to depend on that width. A positive answer must exclude such a shared saving. Improvement at finitely many widths, a randomized algorithm, or a lower bound only under another unproved hypothesis does not by itself meet this criterion. The target is a yes/no assertion about the limit, not its numerical approximation.

The July 2026 preprint improves a fixed-width randomized analysis and does not supply the quantified deterministic refutation. Targeted later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution; its imported inequalities and numerical certificates were not independently verified.

cards.title: Truly subcubic APSP
cards.formal: Is there a constant $\varepsilon>0$ and a uniform randomized algorithm that, for every n-vertex directed graph with real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, outputs all exact shortest-path distances in $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ worst-case time with probability at least \(2/3\)? Use a comparison-addition real RAM: adding, subtracting, and comparing stored real values costs \(O(1)\), and standard arithmetic and bit operations on \(O(\log  n)\)-bit index words cost \(O(1)\). Unreachable distances must be reported as infinity. Arbitrary real-number encodings or unit-cost floor operations are unavailable.
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its adjacency matrix, with a special symbol for absent edges. Output contains one distance for every ordered pair, including zero self-distances. Negative-cycle detection outside the promise is not required. Space and preprocessing are included in the algorithm’s ordinary running time. The probability guarantee applies to the complete output matrix on each fixed input. This is a classical sequential model; quantum and parallel work/depth bounds are separate targets.

cards.title: P versus BPP
cards.formal: Does \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}\)? Precisely, for every language L for which a randomized Turing machine R runs in polynomial time on every input and every random tape, and satisfies $\Pr[R(x)=1_L(x)]\ge2/3$ for every binary string x, does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine deciding L correctly on every x? The polynomial time bound of the deterministic machine may depend on R.
cards.definitions: Input length is \(n=|x|\). A polynomial-time bound means \(C(n+1)^{k}\) steps for fixed constants C,k, independent of x and of the random bits. R uses independent unbiased random bits, at most one fresh bit per computation step, and outputs a single bit. Its error may be on either yes or no inputs, but is bounded separately on each input. P consists of deterministic polynomial-time decision languages and BPP of languages meeting the randomized guarantee above. These are total decision problems, with no excluded promise inputs. No advice, oracle, quantum operations, or input distribution is allowed. The requested deterministic simulation may use a different algorithm; it need not reproduce R's random choices, preserve its precise exponent, or be generated by an effective compiler from R.

cards.title: Optimal explicit pseudorandom generators for read-once branching programs
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants C,D and a uniform family of generators \(G_{n,w,p}:\{0,1\}^{s}\to \{0,1\}^{n}\), for all integers \(n,w\ge 2\) and \(p\ge 1\), with \(s\le C(\log _{2} n+\log _{2} w+p)\), such that \(\left|\Pr_{u\text{ uniform in }\{0,1\}^{s}}[B(G_{n,w,p}(u))=1]-\Pr_{z\text{ uniform in }\{0,1\}^{n}}[B(z)=1]\right|\le2^{-p}\) for every length-n, width-at-most-w ordered read-once branching program B? Require a single deterministic algorithm that, given n,w,p,u and an output position i, computes \(G_{n,w,p}(u)_{i}\) using at most \(D(\log _{2} n+\log _{2} w+p)\) work bits and time \((nw\cdot 2^{p})^{D}\).
cards.definitions: An ordered read-once branching program has layers \(V_{0},\ldots ,V_{n}\), each containing at most w states, a designated initial state in \(V_{0}\), and an accepting subset of \(V_{n}\). For each layer \(i- 1\), each state has one outgoing edge labeled 0 and one labeled 1 to \(V_{i}\). On input z, the program follows the edge labeled \(z_{i}\) at step i and accepts exactly when the final state is accepting. Different edges may merge; neither regularity nor permutation transitions are required. The order is the fixed order \(z_{1},\ldots ,z_{n}\). Programs may be arbitrary nonuniform objects, but the generator cannot inspect their descriptions. The parameters and seed are read-only inputs to the generator algorithm, and the output bit is written separately; all work space, counters and intermediate storage are counted. Seed length is a computable function of the parameters within the stated resources. Uniform seeds induce an ordinary probability distribution, without signed or externally assigned weights. Set \(\varepsilon =2^{- p}\); this dyadic formulation gives the usual \(O(\log (nw/\varepsilon ))\) target for arbitrary positive error by rounding down to a smaller dyadic tolerance.

cards.title: FPT versus \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic algorithm A, a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and an integer \(c\ge0\), such that A decides whether G contains a k-clique and uses at most \(f(k)(N+2)^c\) steps for every encoded pair (G,k) of total bit length N? The exponent c is independent of both k and G. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\) under parameterized many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: A graph G is finite, simple and undirected, with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), including n=0. A k-clique is a subset of exactly k vertices with an edge between each pair of distinct vertices. The empty subset is a 0-clique; no k-clique exists when k>n. For a fixed binary encoding, write \(1^n0\), then the n by n adjacency matrix in row order, then the ordinary binary representation of the nonnegative integer k (0 is written as 0, and otherwise there are no leading zeroes). A valid matrix is symmetric with zero diagonal, and the entire remaining suffix is the representation of k. N counts all bits, including k. A rejects any malformed string in time polynomial in its bit length. The bound in the statement applies to every valid pair, including k>n. The parameter is k alone; there is no promise on density, degree, clique number or any other graph property. A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input and initially blank work tapes; each transition reads or writes only at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The runtime includes parsing, input access and all internal work. Correctness is exact, and no advice, randomness, oracle or quantum operations are supplied. The same A, f and c work for every pair; f must be computable by a machine that halts on every nonnegative integer input, but its growth and the time needed to compute it have no prescribed bound. Constant multiplicative overhead can be absorbed into f. Using full input length rather than n gives the usual FPT question: for k at most n the two lengths are polynomially related, and k>n is rejected after parsing. For completeness, a parameterized language is a set of pairs \((x,k)\in\{0,1\}^*\times\mathbb N\), with both components explicitly encoded. It belongs to FPT if one uniform deterministic machine decides it within \(h(k)(M+2)^a\) steps for a total computable positive h, a fixed nonnegative integer a and complete encoding length M. A parameterized many-one reduction computes a single output pair \((y,k^{\prime})\) in such a time bound, preserves yes versus no membership, and satisfies \(k^{\prime}\le g(k)\) for a total computable function g; writing the output counts toward its runtime. The class W[1] can equivalently be defined as all parameterized languages admitting such a reduction to the Clique problem just specified. This characterization fixes the reduction convention without a change of target. It includes FPT, and Clique belongs to it, so FPT membership of Clique is equivalent to equality of the two classes.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the single algorithm, computable multiplier and constant exponent in the statement, or prove their joint nonexistence. In the affirmative case, prove correctness and the uniform worst-case bound on all pairs, together with the malformed-input convention. In the negative case, exclude every such algorithm, computable f and exponent c; a conditional lower bound, a bound for a restricted algorithm model, or failure at one proposed multiplier and exponent does not settle this target. An algorithm whose polynomial exponent depends on k also does not satisfy the displayed quantifiers.
cards.status_note: The textbook and Bottesch explicitly state the unresolved separation, and the later approximation papers retain it as an assumption. The checked fixed-k algorithm paper and its 2026 publication metadata provide no FPT algorithm. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution; the review does not independently reprove the cited results.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for Densest k-Subgraph
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do there exist a universal constant \(C\ge 1\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm A such that, for every finite simple undirected unweighted graph \(G=(V,E)\) and every integer \(1\le k\le |V|, A(G,k)\) outputs a set \(S\subseteq V\) with |\(S|=k\) and |\(E(G[S])|\ge \operatorname{OPT}(G,k)/C\), where \(\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=\max _{T\subseteq V, |T|=k}|E(G[T])|\)?
cards.definitions: G is explicitly represented by its vertices and edges, and k is supplied in binary as part of the input. \(G[S]\) contains all edges of G with both endpoints in S; loops and parallel edges are absent. The running time is polynomial in the full input length with a fixed exponent independent of k. The same finite C must work for all graphs, all graph sizes and all choices of k; it cannot increase with \(n=|V|\) or with k. The output must be a vertex set, not only an estimate of the optimum. When OPT=0, every k-set meets the requirement. Because all feasible sets have the same cardinality, maximizing edge count, average degree \(2|E(G[S])|/k\), or edges per selected vertex gives the same approximation objective. No promise of a clique, graph expansion, metric edge weights or a random input distribution is supplied. This card fixes deterministic algorithms; a randomized constant-factor guarantee would be major progress but has a distinct derandomization requirement. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The constant-factor algorithm is already ruled out assuming ETH, which remains unproved. The May 2026 primary source explicitly notes the absence of NP-hardness of approximation even at factor 1.001. This card asks about a deterministic constant-factor algorithm on all unweighted graphs, and preserves the distinction between conditional evidence and an unconditional resolution.
