cards.title: Unique Games Conjecture
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every pair of rational constants \(\varepsilon ,\delta >0\) with \(\varepsilon +\delta <1\), does there exist an integer \(q\ge 2\) such that it is NP-hard to distinguish Unique Games instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\varepsilon$ from instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\le\delta$? Here q is the alphabet size, fixed independently of the input graph, and \(\operatorname{val}(G)\) is the largest fraction of constraints simultaneously satisfied by any labeling.
cards.definitions: An instance has finitely many vertices and a nonempty explicit list E of directed edges between distinct vertices; repeated edges are allowed and counted separately. Every vertex receives a label in \([q]=\{1,\ldots ,q\}\). An edge \(e=(u,v)\) carries an explicitly given permutation \(\pi _{e}:[q]\to [q]\) and is satisfied exactly when \(\pi _{e}(\ell (u))=\ell (v)\). Thus \(\operatorname{val}(G)=\max _{\ell} |\){e satisfied by \(\ell\)}|/|E|. There are no graph expansion or degree promises. NP-hardness means a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3SAT mapping every satisfiable formula into the \(\ge 1- \varepsilon\) case and every unsatisfiable formula into the \(\le \delta\) case. The reduction, its running-time exponent, and q may depend on \(\varepsilon ,\delta\). Inputs with value strictly between the thresholds are outside the promise. The question is the NP-hardness proposition itself; \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) is needed when drawing the usual conclusion that no polynomial-time distinguishing algorithm exists. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.title: Deterministic competitiveness of k-server
cards.formal: For each integer \(k\ge 1\), determine \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=\inf\){\(r\ge 1\): for every metric space \((M,d)\) with at least \(k+1\) points and every initial placement \(C_{0}\), there are a deterministic online rule A and a finite \(\beta \ge 0\) such that \(\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma ;C_{0})\le r\cdot \operatorname{OPT}(\sigma ;C_{0})+\beta\) for every finite request sequence \(\sigma\)}. Use the serving model below.
cards.definitions: The metric is symmetric, has finite real distances, is zero exactly on equal points, and satisfies the triangle inequality; the space may be finite or infinite and is known to the online rule. There are exactly k interchangeable, unweighted servers, whose current positions form a multiset. A request \(r_{t}\) must be served before \(r_{t+1}\) is revealed. If a server is already at \(r_{t}\), no movement is needed; otherwise the rule chooses one of the k servers and moves it to \(r_{t}\), paying the metric distance. Restriction to these lazy moves loses no competitive power. A deterministic online rule is a function of the known metric, initial placement and revealed request prefix, with arbitrary memory and no access to future requests; this card imposes no running-time bound. OPT is the minimum total movement cost of an offline rule serving the same finite sequence from \(C_{0}\) with the same k servers and advance knowledge of the sequence. The additive \(\beta\) must be fixed before requests arrive and cannot grow with the number or cost of requests. Randomization, advice about future requests, and extra servers are not supplied. The ratio r depends only on k. The rule and additive constant may depend on the entire metric, \(k, C_{0}\) and r, but not on future requests or sequence length. The classical universal finite upper bounds make the infimum finite. It need not be achieved by one rule at its endpoint.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function g on all integers \(k\ge 1\), and prove in Lean that |\(g- R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)|\le 1/100\) pointwise throughout that domain, in the units stated in the definitions. The answer must establish lower and upper bounds with this uniform error guarantee. An exact determination also qualifies. A finite set of sample values, an uncertified plot, or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit does not determine the curve. No predetermined formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed. This numerical acceptance criterion does not assert exact equality with a conjectured curve.

cards.title: Optimal approximation ratio for unrelated-machine makespan
cards.formal: Determine \(\rho _{\mathrm{unrel}}=\inf\){\(r\ge 1: a\) uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm returns a feasible solution of objective value at most \(r\cdot\)OPT on every unrelated-machine scheduling instance}, in the input and output model below.
cards.definitions: An instance consists of \(m\ge 1\) machines, \(n\ge 0\) independent jobs, and an explicitly given \(m\times n\) matrix of processing times \(p_{ij}\) in the nonnegative rationals or ∞. Rational numerators and denominators are binary encoded; ∞ forbids an assignment. Every job has at least one finite processing time. A schedule is a function \(\sigma :\{1,\ldots ,n\}\to \{1,\ldots ,m\}\) with \(p_{\sigma (j),j}<\infty\). Its makespan is \(Cmax(\sigma )=\max _{i} \sum_{j:\sigma (j)=i} p_{ij}\), and OPT is the minimum of this quantity over all feasible schedules. Jobs are available at time zero, indivisible and processed without interruption on one machine; there are no precedence constraints or communication costs. Jobs assigned to one machine can run consecutively in any order. The algorithm must output \(\sigma\), not merely an estimate of OPT. Its bit running time is polynomial in the entire input length. For each fixed achieved ratio r, the algorithm and its time polynomial are independent of m, n and all processing times; no predictions or promises on matrix structure are supplied. Empty or zero-optimum instances require makespan zero. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object. For each fixed ratio r in the defining set, one finite deterministic algorithm and one time polynomial must work on every instance; both may depend on r. The infimum is over these globally uniform guarantees and need not be attained. There is no per-input-size choice of algorithm, advice or free optimization oracle.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \rho _{\mathrm{unrel}}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture. Any hardness assumption must be stated explicitly; a conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion.
cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The full worst-case constant-improvement question remains open in the checked primary literature. The known \(2- 1/m\) ratio and prediction-assisted results have different quantifiers from the fixed-\(\varepsilon\) target. The \(3/2\) hardness is conditional on \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). cards.title: Planted clique conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following hardness statement true? For every fixed real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), with \(k_n=\lfloor n^{1/2-\varepsilon}\rfloor\), there is no uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) for which \[\Pr[\widehat b=b]\geq\frac23\] in the balanced one-graph experiment below for every sufficiently large integer \(n\).
cards.definitions:
For \(n\geq2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The null distribution \(N_n\) is the distribution of a simple undirected labeled graph on \([n]\) in which each unordered pair of distinct vertices is an edge independently with probability \(1/2\). For \(0\leq k\leq n\), the planted distribution \(P_{n,k}\) chooses \(S\) uniformly among all \(k\)-element subsets of \([n]\), includes every edge inside \(S\), and chooses each other edge independently with probability \(1/2\). There are no loops. The planted set has exactly \(k\) vertices; it is not formed by independently including each vertex.

In the experiment, first choose a fair bit \(b\). If \(b=0\), sample \(G\sim N_n\); if \(b=1\), sample \(G\sim P_{n,k_n}\). Give \(A\) only \((n,k_n,G)\), and let \(\widehat b\in\{0,1\}\) be its output. All randomness of the sampling and of \(A\) is independent. Success is averaged over \(b\), the graph, the planted set when present and the algorithm’s random bits. Writing \(s_A(n,\varepsilon)\) for this probability, \[s_A(n,\varepsilon)=\tfrac12\big(\Pr_{G\sim N_n,A}[A(n,k_n,G)=0]+\Pr_{G\sim P_{n,k_n},A}[A(n,k_n,G)=1]\big).\] This is not a separate \(2/3\) guarantee on each individual graph or on each of the two distributions. The algorithm receives one sampled graph, without the label \(b\), the set \(S\), sample access to the unknown distribution or other side information.

For \(u\geq0\), define \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^a0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(a\) bits and no leading zeroes. The input is \(1^n0\operatorname{code}(k)\), followed by the full \(n^2\) adjacency matrix in row order, with no trailing bits. A valid input has \(n\geq2\), \(0\leq k\leq n\), a symmetric matrix and zero diagonal; let \(L\) be its full bit length. An allowed algorithm is one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and tape alphabet, using fresh independent fair bits and no oracle or advice. For some integers \(C,c\geq1\), on every input and every random-bit sequence it outputs one bit within \(C(L+1)^c\) transitions. Malformed encodings return 0 within this bound. Input processing, bit arithmetic and any additional graphs generated by the algorithm count toward time. On valid inputs \(L=\Theta(n^2)\), so polynomial time in \(L\) and in \(n\) are equivalent.

For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), the forbidden guarantee is \(\exists A,C,c,N\ \forall n\geq N:\ s_A(n,\varepsilon)\geq2/3\), with the global clock condition just specified. The program and constants may depend on this fixed \(\varepsilon\), but cannot change with \(n\); \(\varepsilon\) is not supplied as an oracle or an infinite advice string. The supplied integer \(k_n\) removes any need to compute a real power to construct the input. The conjecture therefore says that every allowed algorithm has success below \(2/3\) for arbitrarily large \(n\), for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). It does not assert that its success tends to \(1/2\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of this hardness proposition or its logical negation. To refute it, give some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), one allowed polynomial-time algorithm and a proof that its balanced success is at least \(2/3\) for every sufficiently large \(n\). To prove it, exclude every such algorithm for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). Success only on infinitely many sizes does not satisfy the refutation target. A limitation on sum-of-squares relaxations, local searches or another restricted model does not establish hardness against all allowed machines. A recovery result must imply the stated detection guarantee; a change of planting distribution or a conditional theorem must not be treated as an unconditional resolution of this exact experiment.
cards.status_note: No unconditional proof or unrestricted polynomial-time refutation of this exact fixed-size, balanced constant-success hypothesis was located in a bounded check through 14 September 2026. The cited sum-of-squares theorem is a relaxation/refutation lower bound; the optimal-advantage and September 2026 topology results are conditional, and several newer recovery results use other random graph models. Source/model review does not independently certify every cited proof.

cards.title: Average-case NP hardness from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.definitions: A sampler is one randomized Turing machine S which, given \(1^{n}\), halts within \(q(n)\) steps on every random tape for a fixed polynomial q. Its output distribution \(D_{n}\) is over finite binary strings \(x; |x|\le q(n)\), and n is the ensemble parameter, not necessarily |x|. Sampling is exact with independent unbiased coin flips, and S has no advice or oracle. An exact decider A receives \((1^{n},x)\), halts, and returns the membership bit of L correctly for every n and x. Write \(T_{A}(1^{n},x)\) for its running time. The pair \((\mathrm{L},D)\) belongs to AvgP if there exist such an \(A, \varepsilon >0, C>0\), and integer \(k\ge 1\) with $\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}[T_A(1^n,x)^\varepsilon]\le C(n+1)^k$ for every \(n\ge 1\). The constants and A may depend on L and S but not on n. This moment definition is the robust Levin notion, not the requirement that the first moment itself be polynomial. The algorithm is deterministic and never gives a wrong answer; difficult inputs may take a long time. NP uses ordinary polynomially bounded certificates and deterministic polynomial-time verification. Both the hard language and its sampler must be fixed across all input lengths.

cards.title: Rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics with \(\Delta +2\) colours
cards.formal: Do absolute constants \(C,c>0\) exist such that, for every finite simple n-vertex graph G with maximum degree \(\Delta\) and every integer \(q\ge \Delta +2\), the single-vertex heat-bath Glauber chain on proper q-colourings has total-variation mixing time \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le Cn^{c}\)?
cards.definitions: Let \(n\ge 1\) and \(\Omega\)={\(\sigma :V(G)\to [q] : \sigma (u)\ne \sigma (v)\) for every edge uv}. Colours are labelled; unused colours are allowed. At each discrete step choose v uniformly from \(V(G)\), then choose a colour uniformly from \([q]\)\\(\{\sigma (u):u\in N(v)\}\) and assign it to v, leaving all other vertices unchanged. The current colour is among the available choices. Let P be this transition matrix and \(\pi\) the uniform distribution on \(\Omega\). Define \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)=\min \{t\in Z_{\ge 0}: \max _{\sigma \in \Omega} (1/2)\sum_{\tau \in \Omega}|\mathrm{P}^{t}(\sigma ,\tau )- \pi (\tau )|\le 1/4\}\). This counts individual vertex updates, not sweeps or bit operations. The constants C,c must be independent of \(n, \Delta , q\) and G. The initial proper colouring is arbitrary, and the graph has no girth, treewidth or randomness promise. This card fixes a uniform polynomial bound across degrees, rather than leaving the exponent’s parameter dependence implicit.

cards.title: Kannan–Tetali–Vempala conjecture
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(K,c>0\) exist such that, for all \(r,s\ge 1\) and all nonnegative integer margins \(a\in \mathbb{N} ^{r},b\in \mathbb{N} ^{s}\) with a nonempty realization set \(\Omega (a,b)\), the lazy switch chain below satisfies \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le K(r+s)^{c}\)?
cards.definitions: For integers \(r,s\ge1\), let \(a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{r}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{s}\). The promised nonempty set \(\Omega(a,b)\) consists of binary matrices \(M\in\{0,1\}^{r\times s}\) with row sums \(a_i\) and column sums \(b_j\). At each attempted transition independently, stay with probability \(1/2\). Otherwise choose an unordered pair of distinct rows uniformly and an unordered pair of distinct columns uniformly and independently. If their rectangle has either alternating pattern \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) or \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), replace it by the other; otherwise stay. If \(r<2\) or \(s<2\), the state space is a singleton and the chain stays. Let \(P\) be the transition matrix and \(\pi\) the uniform distribution on \(\Omega(a,b)\). For an integer \(t\ge0\), define \(d(t)=\max_{M\in\Omega(a,b)}\frac12\sum_{N\in\Omega(a,b)}|P^t(M,N)-1/|\Omega(a,b)||\). Let \(t_{\rm mix}(1/4)=\min\{t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:d(t)\le1/4\}\), or \(+\infty\) if this set is empty. Time counts attempted transitions, including holds. The polynomial bound must use the same constants for every dimension and feasible pair of margins, without density, regularity or balance assumptions. This is a mathematical mixing-time question, with no requirement on bit complexity or implementation of a sampler.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that universal constants \(K,c>0\) bound the specified worst-case mixing time by \(K(r+s)^c\) for every nonempty binary-margin state space, or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every such pair of constants there are feasible dimensions and margins violating that bound. The theorem must concern the exact lazy chain and every starting matrix defined here.

cards.title: FPRAS for counting perfect matchings
cards.formal: Does there exist a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for the number \(Z(G)\) of perfect matchings in every finite undirected simple graph G? More precisely, is there one randomized algorithm A and one polynomial p such that, for every explicitly encoded graph G and rational \(0<\varepsilon <1, A\) halts within \(p(\mathrm{L},\lceil 1/\varepsilon \rceil )\) bit operations and outputs a nonnegative rational Ẑ satisfying \(\Pr [(1- \varepsilon )Z(G)\le \hat\{Z\}\le (1+\varepsilon )Z(G)]\ge 3/4\), where L is the total binary input length?
cards.definitions: A matching is a set of edges with no shared endpoints. It is perfect if every vertex is incident to exactly one selected edge. \(Z(G)\) is the number of distinct such edge sets; edges and vertices are unweighted. The graph is specified by a labeled vertex set and its full edge list, without bipartiteness, density, degree, expansion or planarity promises. For an odd number of vertices \(Z(G)=0\); for the empty graph \(Z(G)=1\). The random bits are independent fair bits, all computational and output costs are counted, and the time bound holds for every random tape. When \(Z(G)=0\), require output zero with probability one; this causes no loss of generality because existence of a perfect matching can be decided deterministically in polynomial time before approximation begins. The fixed success probability \(3/4\) can be amplified to \(1- \delta\) by independent repetitions and a median, with an \(O(\log (1/\delta ))\) multiplicative overhead. The same polynomial p must work for all graphs and all requested accuracies. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.title: FPRAS for #BIS
cards.formal: Does \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\), counting all independent sets in an arbitrary finite simple bipartite graph, admit a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme? Precisely, do there exist one probabilistic Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(C,k\geq1\) such that, for every encoded bipartite graph \(G\) and rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), the machine outputs a nonnegative rational \(\widehat Z\) within \(C(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil)^k\) steps on every random tape and satisfies \[\Pr\big[(1-\varepsilon)Z(G)\leq\widehat Z\leq(1+\varepsilon)Z(G)\big]\geq\tfrac34?\] Here \(Z(G)\) is the number of independent vertex subsets, \(L\) is the complete encoded input length, and the probability is over the algorithm’s independent fair coin bits.
cards.definitions: For an integer \(n\geq0\), the vertex set is \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), partitioned into disjoint specified sets \(U,V\), either of which may be empty. An edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices with one endpoint in each part; there are no loops or parallel edges. An independent set is a subset \(I\subseteq U\cup V\) that contains no complete edge, and \(Z(G)=|\{I\subseteq U\cup V:I\text{ is independent}\}|\). Every independent set is counted once, with weight one, irrespective of its size or the number of its vertices in either part. The empty set is included, so \(Z(G)\geq1\), and the graph with no vertices has \(Z(G)=1\). Graphs may be disconnected and have isolated vertices, arbitrary degrees and parts of unequal sizes. Fix the following explicit finite-alphabet encoding. Write bin(j) for the binary expansion of a nonnegative integer j, with no leading zeros except in bin(0). An input is the string bin(n)#b#a#bin(r)#bin(s), where b has exactly n bits specifying part membership, a has exactly n(n−1)/2 bits specifying adjacency for pairs (i,j), i<j, in increasing lexicographic order, and integers r,s satisfy 0<r<s. Every adjacency bit equal to one must join vertices whose membership bits differ. The accuracy is \(\varepsilon=r/s\); the fraction need not be reduced. Thus isolated vertices are represented explicitly, and L counts all bits and separators, including both accuracy integers. The ceiling \(\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\) is taken after real division. An output encodes \(\widehat Z=p/q\) as bin(p)#bin(q), with integers \(p\geq0\), \(q\geq1\). The machine has finite control and finitely many ordinary work tapes, with a stream of independent unbiased random bits. All input reading, bit computation, random-bit access and output writing are charged as Turing-machine steps; exact arithmetic on unbounded integers or reals is not a unit-cost operation. There is no oracle, advice, quantum resource or random input-graph assumption. The same program and constants C,k must work for all graph sizes, degrees, bipartitions and accuracies. Malformed strings are rejected by returning 0/1 within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps on every random tape, after increasing the common constants if needed. Deterministic algorithms are permitted as the special case that ignores the random bits.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that a single algorithm and constants C,k meet the stated worst-case bit-cost bound, rational-output requirement and per-instance relative-error guarantee, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm and constants exist. The negative direction must rule out every uniform fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme. Equivalently, every candidate satisfying the polynomial runtime and output conditions must have some valid input \((G,\varepsilon)\) on which its probability of a correct relative approximation is strictly less than \(3/4\). Showing a failure of a particular sampler, a finite running-time lower bound, or difficulty of exact counting does not establish this universal impossibility. A conditional lower bound, for example one assuming \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\), is not an unconditional negative resolution unless the assumed separation is also proved. The positive direction must cover every input graph and every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), with a polynomial degree independent of those inputs; expected runtime alone does not match the specified bound without a proof yielding the required always-bounded scheme. The target is existence of an approximation algorithm with its requested accuracy parameter, so a fixed numerical tolerance of 1/100 does not replace the quantified relative-error requirement. A deterministic fully polynomial scheme would meet the target, but is not required.

cards.title: Hadwiger’s conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following proposition true? For every integer \(n\ge1\), every simple undirected graph \(G\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and every integer \(t\ge1\), if \(\chi(G)\ge t\), then \(G\) contains \(K_t\) as an ordinary graph minor. Equivalently, \(h(G)\ge\chi(G)\) for every such graph, where \(h\) is the Hadwiger number defined below.
cards.definitions: The edge set of \(G\) is any set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices in \([n]\); there are no loops or parallel edges. For an integer \(r\ge1\), a proper \(r\)-coloring is a map \(c:[n]\to\{1,\ldots,r\}\) such that \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is the least such \(r\); it exists and lies between \(1\) and \(n\). The graph \(K_t\) has \(t\) vertices and every possible edge. A \(K_t\) minor in \(G\) means that there are \(t\) pairwise disjoint nonempty vertex sets \(B_1,\ldots,B_t\) with both of the following properties: for every \(i\), any two vertices of \(B_i\) are joined by a finite path of edges of \(G\) whose vertices all lie in \(B_i\); and for every \(i<j\), some edge of \(G\) has one endpoint in \(B_i\) and one in \(B_j\). A singleton is connected. The branch sets may have any sizes, need not cover all vertices, and have no restrictions on extra internal edges or on parity. This is equivalent to obtaining \(K_t\) by vertex deletions, edge deletions and edge contractions, discarding loops and merging parallel edges after contraction. It is neither an induced-minor nor an odd-minor requirement. The Hadwiger number \(h(G)\) is the largest \(t\) admitting these branch sets, so \(1\le h(G)\le n\). For \(t\ge2\), the proposition equivalently says that absence of a \(K_t\) minor implies a proper \((t-1)\)-coloring; the \(t=1\) assertion holds automatically for a nonempty graph. Relabeling vertices has no effect. The quantifiers impose no connectedness, degree, order or other restriction on \(G\), and no running-time bound on finding a coloring or a minor.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition for all finite nonempty simple undirected graphs and all integers \(t\ge1\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: existence of a finite graph \(G\) and integer \(t\ge1\) with \(\chi(G)\ge t\) and no \(t\) branch sets satisfying the definition. A counterexample must certify both the chromatic lower bound and absence of the ordinary clique minor. A proof of \(h(G)\ge\chi(G)\) for every graph is an equivalent positive answer. No efficient algorithm is required. A constant-factor or asymptotic coloring bound, a finite list of established values of \(t\), a restricted graph class, or a counterexample only to the odd-minor variant does not cover the target.
cards.status_note: The ordinary Hadwiger conjecture is explicitly open in Liu–Luo v2 of 9 September 2026, still its latest arXiv version on 14 September. Its triple-logarithmic coloring theorem is a recent preprint claim, not independently verified here. The December 2025 disproof and its September 2026 citation concern the stronger odd-minor version. Checked source formulations and a bounded later-work search do not certify all cited proofs.

cards.title: Deterministic linear-time minimum spanning tree
cards.formal: Is there one deterministic comparison-based algorithm that, on every connected simple undirected graph with n vertices, m edges and arbitrary real edge weights, outputs a minimum spanning tree in \(O(m+n)\) worst-case time in the comparison RAM model below?
cards.definitions: The graph is explicitly supplied as vertex and edge records, with vertices numbered \(1,\ldots ,n\) and edges given distinct identifiers. An edge record contains its two endpoints and a weight key representing an arbitrary real number. A spanning tree is a set T of \(n- 1\) edges connecting all vertices without a cycle; it is minimum when \(\sum_{e\in T}w(e)\) is smallest among all spanning trees. For \(n=1\) the output is empty. Equal and negative weights are permitted, and any minimum tree is acceptable. Weight keys may be copied and compared, but their bit representations cannot be inspected, and arithmetic on their numerical values is unavailable. Each comparison has unit cost. Nonweight data, addresses and indices use \(O(\log (m+n+2))\)-bit words on a random-access machine, with unit-cost reads, writes, comparisons, standard word arithmetic, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts; arithmetic is restricted to these words. All ordinary operations count in the running time, not just weight comparisons. The algorithm has a fixed finite description and no input-length-dependent advice or free precomputed tables. Any tables it constructs, as well as writing the output, are charged to its time. The hidden linear-time constant must be independent of graph topology, n,m and the weights. This fixes a conventional uniform sequential comparison model. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.title: Dynamic optimality conjecture
cards.formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree \(T_{0}\) and every X, \(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\)? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.
cards.definitions: Keys are \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 1\), ordered by their integer values. A binary search tree has one node per key, every key in a left subtree smaller than its root and every key in a right subtree larger. A rotation on a parent-child edge exchanges those two nodes while reattaching the intermediate subtree so that the order is preserved. To splay a requested key x, repeatedly apply the following bottom-up rule until x is root. If its parent is root, rotate the edge from x to its parent (zig). Otherwise let p be its parent and g its grandparent. If x and p are both left children or both right children, first rotate p above g and then x above p (zig-zig). Otherwise rotate x above p and then x above g (zig-zag). Each access costs one plus its number of rotations. The tree after the access is the initial tree for the next access. For a finite sequence \(X\in [n]*, \operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})\) is the sum of these costs starting from \(T_{0}\). A comparator execution may start with any tree, knows X in full, and serves each request by any finite sequence of parent-child rotations anywhere in the current tree whose final root is the requested key. Its cost is the same one-plus-rotations sum. \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) is the minimum cost over all such initial trees and executions; it is zero for the empty sequence. There are no insertions, deletions or additional node operations. This root-BST cost convention is the one used in the saved source, with the additive n term accounting for the initial tree.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that one finite constant C bounds \(\operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})/(\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n)\) for all n, all initial trees \(T_{0}\) and all finite access sequences X, or prove that this ratio is unbounded over those inputs. A counterexample to a particular proposed value of C alone does not refute the universal-constant claim.
cards.status_note: The July 2026 primary preprint gives a growing competitive factor and still distinguishes its theorem from constant dynamic optimality. The primary text and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026; no complete resolution was found in that check. This review does not independently verify the new proof.

cards.title: Superlogarithmic static cell-probe lower bounds
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed integer \(k\ge 2\) and a uniformly polynomial-time computable family of Boolean functions \(F_{n}\) on an n-word database and a \(k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil\)-bit query such that its optimal deterministic static cell-probe query complexity \(t*F(n)\), with word size \(\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\) memory cells, satisfies \(t*F(n)/\log _{2} n\to \infty\) as \(n\to \infty\)?
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge 2\) put \(w=\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) and \(s=n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\). A database is \(D\in (\{0,1\}^{w})^{n}, a\) query is \(q\in \{0,1\}^{k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil}\), and \(F_{n}(D,q)\in \{0,1\}\). Explicit means that a single deterministic Turing machine computes \(F_{n}(D,q)\), given \((1^{n},D,q)\), in time polynomial in n; no advice is allowed in this definition. A data structure may preprocess D by any map \(E_{n}\) into s cells of w bits each. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and this encoding may be nonlinear and nonuniform. For each query, a deterministic adaptive decision tree reads cells, choosing the next address from the query and previously read contents, and must output \(F_{n}(D,q)\) exactly for every database. Computation between probes is free. The trees may depend on n, F and the query, but their only access to D is through \(E_{n}(D)\). Each query starts without free database-dependent private information; memory is static and read-only. Define \(t*F(n)\) as the minimum, over all such encodings and trees, of the maximum number of probes over all D and q. All memory cells count toward s. This card fixes a near-linear-space, short-query, one-bit-answer specialization of the broader static lower-bound challenge; it does not assert equivalence to every space or word-size variant.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed k and admissible uniform family F satisfy: for every real \(B>0\) there is N such that \(t*F(n)>B \log _{2} n\) for every \(n\ge N\). Alternatively, prove the exact negation: for every fixed k and every admissible family F, there is a finite \(B>0\) such that \(t*F(n)\le B \log _{2} n\) for arbitrarily large n. In particular, the negative answer need not establish an \(O(\log  n)\) bound for all sufficiently large n.
cards.status_note: Primary sources and later-result searches checked on 11 September 2026 did not supply a resolution of the stated static specialization. The STOC 2026 paper retains the broader static barrier as Open Problem 1.1. The fixed near-linear space, short-query Boolean output and uniform polynomial-time family are an expressly recorded specialization; conditional proof barriers and bounds for dynamic memory or superpolynomial query sets do not resolve it.

cards.title: Deterministic fully dynamic connectivity with polylogarithmic worst-case updates
cards.formal: Does there exist a single deterministic data structure and fixed constants \(C,c,d>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge 2\), an initially empty undirected simple graph on vertex set \([n]\) can be maintained under any online sequence of edge insertions, edge deletions and pairwise connectivity queries, using at most \(C n^{d}\) words of memory and at most \(C(\log _{2} n)^{c}\) time for each individual operation? Initialization may take at most \(C n^{d}\) time and depends only on n. All connectivity answers must be exact in the word-RAM model specified below.
cards.definitions: An insertion \(insert(u,v)\) adds a previously absent unordered edge \(\{u,v\}\), where \(u\ne v; a\) deletion \(delete(u,v)\) removes an existing edge. A query \(connected(u,v)\) returns whether the current graph contains a path from u to v, with \(connected(u,u)\)=true. Updates are valid, arrive one at a time and must finish before the next operation is revealed. No future operations or advance description of the sequence is supplied. The data structure must work for every finite sequence, including sequences chosen in response to its previous behavior. The word RAM has word size \(w=\lceil a \log _{2} n\rceil\) for a fixed constant a large enough to address its polynomial space. Unit-cost instructions are indirect reads/writes, word addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient/remainder, comparisons, Boolean bit operations and shifts; arithmetic results stored in one word are reduced modulo 2ʷ where appropriate. Arbitrary-precision computation costs its constituent word operations. All maintenance, rebuilding and query work is charged to the operation performing it. The exponent c is independent of n and of the length or contents of the operation sequence. The graph is unrestricted apart from being undirected and simple; no planarity, bounded-degree or expansion promise is given.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

Deterministic subpolynomial worst-case bounds and polylogarithmic amortized bounds are already known.

cards.title: Fully dynamic near-optimal matching with polylogarithmic updates
cards.formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), is there a randomized fully dynamic algorithm that maintains an explicit matching M with |\(M|\ge \nu (G)/(1+\varepsilon )\) in every current general graph G using polylogarithmic expected amortized update time against an oblivious adversary?
cards.definitions: The graph is simple, undirected and unweighted, on the fixed vertex set \([n], n\ge 2; \nu (G)\) is its maximum matching cardinality. It starts empty. An update inserts one absent edge or deletes one present edge. Updates arrive online, but the entire valid sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits and is not revealed in advance. More precisely, for every fixed \(\varepsilon\) and constant \(a\ge 1\), require constants K,d,B and a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon ,a}\) such that every sequence of \(T\le n^{a}\) updates has expected total initialization-plus-update cost at most \(K[n+T(\log _{2}(n+2))^{d}]\). Words have \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits; standard word operations, memory access and retained random bits are charged. With probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\), after every update in the sequence an explicit mate array represents a valid matching satisfying the approximation bound. Reading a vertex’s mate or the matching cardinality takes \(O(1)\) time; enumerating all matching edges costs \(O(n)\) and need not occur after every update. Changes to the mate array count toward update cost. Constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and a, but not on n, T or the sequence. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), adaptive-adversary guarantee or worst-case per-update bound is required. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) (or \(\Theta (\log  N)\) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No polylogarithmic-update algorithm meeting the fixed-accuracy, explicit-matching target was found. Matching-size estimators, ordered-RS-dependent bounds and the 2026 maximal-matching improvement do not resolve it.

cards.title: Worst-case sample complexity of trace reconstruction
cards.formal: For every fixed deletion probability \(\delta \in (0,1)\), determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to \infty , N_{\delta}(n)\): the least number of independent deletion traces that permit exact reconstruction of every unknown n-bit string with success probability at least \(2/3\), with no processing-time bound.
cards.definitions: For \(x\in \{0,1\}^{n}, a\) deletion trace is generated by independently retaining each input bit with probability \(1- \delta\) and concatenating the retained bits in their original order. Let \(\mu _{x,\delta}\) be its probability distribution on ⋃_\(\{k=0\}^{n}\{0,1\}^{k}\). Different traces use independent deletion masks. The estimator is given \(n, \delta\) and m independent samples from \(\mu _{x,\delta}\); it receives neither deletion positions nor direct access to x. Its output is an element of \(\{0,1\}^{n}\), and success means equality to the entire original string. One estimator for the given n and \(\delta\) must succeed for every x with probability at least \(2/3\) over the traces and any internal randomness. There is no restriction on processing time, storage, description length or computation between observations: this card asks an information-theoretic sample-complexity question. Formally, let \(N_{\delta}(n)\) be the smallest integer m for which such an estimator exists. The requested asymptotic constants may depend on \(\delta\), but not on n or x. The value is finite because a trace of length n reveals the entire string, and this event has positive probability \((1- \delta )^{n}\). The string is adversarially chosen and has no codebook, sparsity, separation, randomness or other structural promise. Traces are ordinary linear subsequences without cyclic shifts.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(f_{\delta}(n)\) and, for every fixed \(\delta \in (0,1)\), constants \(0<c_{\delta}\le C_{\delta}<\infty\) such that \(c_{\delta} f_{\delta}(n)\le N_{\delta}(n)\le C_{\delta} f_{\delta}(n)\) for all \(n\ge 2\), allowing finitely many small n to be absorbed into the constants. Prove both the reconstruction guarantee and the worst-case information-theoretic lower bound in Lean. The dependence on n must be determined within constant factors; deciding only whether a polynomial number of traces suffices does not necessarily determine it.
cards.status_note: The July 2026 quasipolynomial sample theorem supersedes the saved 2025 general upper frontier but does not give polynomially many traces. The best unrestricted lower bound cited remains polynomial; circular and local-SQ bounds concern different models. Checked through 11 September 2026.

Success is required separately for every input pair. Output only the distance estimate; an edit script is not required. The constants C,K,d,B are fixed independently of n and the strings. There is no promise about the distance, repetitions or input distribution, and no additive error is allowed. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.title: Constant-factor universally truthful auctions for submodular bidders
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge 1\) and a randomized, universally truthful combinatorial-auction mechanism that, for every number n of bidders, number m of items and normalized monotone submodular valuation profile, uses polynomial communication and produces an allocation of expected social welfare at least OPT/C?
cards.definitions: There are \(m\ge 1\) distinct indivisible items and \(n\ge 1\) bidders. Bidder i privately knows \(v_{i}:2^{[m]}\to Q_{\ge 0}\), with \(v_{i}(\varnothing )=0, v_{i}(S)\le v_{i}(T)\) for \(S\subseteq T\), and \(v_{i}(S)+v_{i}(T)\ge v_{i}(S\cup T)+v_{i}(S\cap T)\) for all S,T. To make communication in bits precise, a public integer \(B\ge 1\) bounds the binary lengths of the numerator and positive denominator of each value. This is a bound per value, not permission to transmit the exponential table. One uniform protocol must work for every n,m,B with at most \(\mathrm{P}(n,m,B)\) communicated bits in the worst case, for one fixed polynomial P. Arbitrary interactive messages and demand queries are allowed; all query descriptions, replies, allocations and payments count toward communication. Local computation by bidders and auctioneer is unrestricted but must terminate. An outcome consists of pairwise disjoint bundles \(S_{1},\ldots ,S_{n}\) and rational payments \(p_{1},\ldots ,p_{n}\); unallocated items are allowed. Utilities are quasilinear, \(u_{i}=v_{i}(S_{i})- p_{i}\). There are no private budgets or distributional assumptions. Universal truthfulness means the mechanism is a report-independent distribution over deterministic dominant-strategy truthful mechanisms: for every fixed random seed r, every i, every admissible true and alternative reported type \(v_{i},v_{i}'\), and every \(v_{- i}, v_{i}(S_{i}(v_{i},v_{- i};r))- p_{i}(v_{i},v_{- i};r)\ge v_{i}(S_{i}(v_{i}' ,v_{- i};r))- p_{i}(v_{i}' ,v_{- i};r)\). A low-communication protocol implements this outcome and payment rule on the distributed reported types. OPT=\(\max  \sum_{i} v_{i}(T_{i})\), where the maximum is over pairwise disjoint \(T_{i}\subseteq [m]\). The expected welfare guarantee holds for every truthful valuation profile, with expectation only over the mechanism’s randomness; C is independent of n,m,B. No additional individual-rationality or transfer-sign restriction is imposed in this formulation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.status_note: The checked primary literature retains a gap between constant nontruthful welfare approximation and the general universally truthful guarantee. cards.title: Existence of complete EFX allocations for additive valuations
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: For all integers \(n\ge4\) and \(m\ge0\), and every matrix \((v_{ig})_{i\in[n],g\in[m]}\) of nonnegative real values, does there exist a complete allocation \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) such that \(\sum_{h\in A_i}v_{ih}\ge\sum_{h\in A_j\setminus\{g\}}v_{ih}\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\) and every \(g\in A_j\) satisfying \(v_{ig}>0\)?
cards.definitions: For an integer \(k\ge0\), write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). There are \(n\) agents and \(m\) indivisible goods. The finite nonnegative real number \(v_{ig}\) is agent \(i\)'s value for good \(g\); her value for a bundle \(S\subseteq[m]\) is \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\). A complete allocation is an ordered partition \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) into pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is \([m]\); empty bundles are allowed and every good is allocated exactly once. Envy-freeness up to any positively valued good (EFX) means that, for all agents \(i,j\) and all \(g\in A_j\) with \(v_{ig}>0\), one has \(v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})\). Both the positivity test and the comparison use agent \(i\)'s valuation. If all goods in \(A_j\) have value zero for \(i\), there is no inequality for that pair. Values need not be rational or strictly positive. No payments, chores, discarded goods, randomized allocations, or efficiency requirement are present. This uses the positive-good convention of Definition 5 in the cited survey; the stronger per-allocation condition EFX-zero also tests goods with value zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence for every valuation matrix in the stated domain, or prove its negation in Lean: there are finite \(n\ge4\), \(m\ge0\), and nonnegative additive valuations for which every complete partition violates at least one of the stated EFX inequalities. The target is existence, with no algorithmic, efficiency or stronger fairness requirement.
cards.status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. No resolution of the complete-allocation question for unrestricted nonnegative additive valuations was located. The August 2026 result covers four agents and at most nine goods; nonadditive counterexamples do not meet this model. The certificate corpus and cited proofs were not independently rerun.

cards.title: Matrix multiplication exponent
cards.formal: Determine, with the absolute \(1/100\) acceptance precision below, the matrix multiplication exponent \(\omega=\inf\{\tau\in\mathbb R:\exists C>0\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge2\Rightarrow s(n)\le Cn^\tau\}\). Here s(n) is the minimum number of arithmetic gates in a circuit computing all entries of the product of two arbitrary n by n complex matrices exactly, in the model below.
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge2\), the inputs are the \(2n^2\) independent complex variables \(a_{ij},b_{ij}\), with \(1\le i,j\le n\). The required n squared outputs are the polynomials \(c_{ij}=\sum_{t=1}^n a_{it}b_{tj}\). A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose source nodes are input variables or constants from \(\mathbb C\), and whose other nodes have two ordered inputs and apply addition, subtraction or multiplication. Multiple uses of a previously computed value are allowed. Each ordered output position (i,j) designates a node whose polynomial is exactly c_ij, so one circuit must be correct on every pair of complex matrices. Circuit topology and constants may depend on n, but not on the matrix entries. Size is the number of arithmetic gates, including gates operating on constants; source nodes and output designations have zero cost. No division, comparison, branching, randomness, approximation or test of the input values is permitted. This is a nonuniform algebraic model: a separate finite circuit may be chosen for each n, with no required algorithm generating the circuits or their constants. Scalar arithmetic is exact, and costs of representing complex numbers in bits are outside the model. The number of gates differs only by a constant factor from the source’s binary-circuit wire measure, and allowing an explicit subtraction gate also changes size by at most a constant factor; neither changes the exponent. Define s(n) as the least size among correct circuits. This minimum exists because the elementary multiplication formula gives a circuit, and sizes are nonnegative integers. The n squared output polynomials are distinct and none is a source polynomial, so each needs a distinct arithmetic gate and \(s(n)\ge n^2\). The elementary upper bound \(s(n)\le2n^3\) makes the exponent set nonempty and gives \(2\le\omega\le3\). The infimum need not be attained. Specifically, \(\omega\le u\) means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a real \(C_\varepsilon>0\) such that \(s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{u+\varepsilon}\) for every integer n at least two. A lower bound \(\omega\ge\ell\) means that for every real \(\tau<\ell\) and C>0 there is an integer n at least two with \(s(n)>Cn^\tau\). These quantified bounds do not demand a circuit family attaining the endpoint exponent or a pointwise lower bound at that endpoint. The source’s conjecture \(\omega=2\) is one possible value of the numerical target selected for this card.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real number a by an unambiguous mathematical description and give a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|a-\omega|\le1/100\) for the unrestricted circuit quantity above. Equivalently, certify bounds \(\ell\le\omega\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le1/50\) and take \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). A proved exact value also qualifies. The proof must justify both sides of the error interval, with the infimum and nonattainment conventions in the definitions. Merely copying or renaming the defining infimum, reporting an optimized upper bound, or giving a bound only for a restricted tensor method does not meet the requirement. This tolerance concerns the value of the exponent and does not assert a proof of the exact conjecture that omega equals two.
cards.status_note: The checked source states the exponent-two conjecture, and the August 2026 papers report improved upper bounds without determining omega. The known interval displayed here remains wider than the requested numerical tolerance. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified determination at that precision. The optimization certificate was not independently replayed, and its repository was still described as in preparation in the checked version.

cards.title: Permanent versus determinant
cards.formal: Over \(\mathbb C\), is the determinantal complexity of the permanent not bounded above by any polynomial? Precisely, writing \(d_n=\operatorname{dc}_{\mathbb C}(\operatorname{perm}_n)\) as defined below, is it true that for every triple of integers \(B,k,N\ge1\) there is an integer \(n\ge N\) with \(d_n>B(n+1)^k\)? The matrices in the definition are unrestricted exact affine-linear representations over \(\mathbb C\).
cards.definitions: For an integer \(n\ge1\), let \(X=(x_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) consist of \(n^2\) algebraically independent commuting variables over \(\mathbb C\). Let \(S_n\) be the set of all permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and set \(\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n x_{i,\sigma(i)}\). For any \(m\times m\) matrix \(M\) over a commutative ring, \(\det(M)=\sum_{\pi\in S_m}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{a=1}^m M_{a,\pi(a)}\), where \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=(-1)^{|\{(a,b):a<b,\ \pi(a)>\pi(b)\}|}\). Define \(d_n\) to be the least integer \(m\ge1\) for which there exist constant matrices \(A_0,A_{ij}\in\mathbb C^{m\times m}\), one \(A_{ij}\) for each input variable, such that \[\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\det\!\left(A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}A_{ij}\right)\] as an identity in \(\mathbb C[x_{ij}:1\le i,j\le n]\). Thus every entry is a constant plus an arbitrary complex linear combination of all input variables. Equality means equality of every coefficient, equivalently equality for every complex assignment, not just Boolean assignments. Finite representations exist, so the minimum is defined; for example the known bound \(d_n\le2^n-1\) suffices. The resource is the matrix dimension \(m\), not its number of entries, coefficient bit lengths or time to find the matrices. Constants can be arbitrary complex numbers, independently for each \(n\), with no computability or uniform construction requirement. Variables may be reused in any number of entries. No symmetry, sparsity, rank condition on \(A_0\), sign restriction, read-once property or restriction on cancellation is imposed. A limit of determinants is not an exact representation unless some permitted matrix already has determinant equal to the permanent. Since every \(d_n\) is finite, the formal assertion is equivalent to nonexistence of integers \(B,k\ge1\) satisfying \(d_n\le B(n+1)^k\) for all \(n\ge1\): finitely many exceptions to an upper bound can be absorbed into \(B\). The stated lower-bound quantifiers require arbitrarily large violating indices for every proposed polynomial, not eventual domination of that polynomial at every sufficiently large index.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the quantified lower-bound proposition, or of its logical negation: there exist integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that for every \(n\ge1\) there exist an integer \(1\le m\le B(n+1)^k\) and complex matrices \(A_0,A_{ij}\) satisfying the exact polynomial identity above. A negative answer may prove existence of this nonuniform family without an algorithm to generate its constants. A positive answer must exclude all allowed affine-linear matrices for the relevant \(n,m\), including those that break the permanent’s symmetries. A fixed-degree polynomial lower bound, a bound restricted to real coefficients or a restricted matrix class, or a lower bound for a different polynomial does not prove the proposition. A polynomial-size limiting representation alone does not refute this exact target.

Symmetry restrictions, real-field bounds, border upper bounds and Boolean-sum simple projections are not substituted for this card’s exact model.

cards.title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) that, on every input encoding a polynomial \(f\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\ldots,X_m]\) with \(m\geq1\), halts and outputs YES exactly when \[\exists(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m\quad f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0,\] and outputs NO otherwise? The number of variables, degree and coefficients are unrestricted finite input data, and there is no time or space efficiency requirement.
cards.definitions:
The field \(\mathbb Q\) consists of exact fractions \(a/b\), with \(a\in\mathbb Z\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), identifying fractions of the same value; addition and multiplication are the usual exact field operations. A polynomial input describes \(f=\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_j\prod_{i=1}^{m}X_i^{e_{ji}}\), with \(r\geq0\), \(a_j\in\mathbb Z\) and \(e_{ji}\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Repeated monomials and zero coefficients are allowed. The empty sum is the zero polynomial and \(X_i^0=1\), including when evaluating at zero. Constants are represented with all exponents zero. A rational zero is any tuple in \(\mathbb Q^m\) giving exact value zero; there is no bound on its numerators or denominators and no integrality restriction.

Use the following explicit effective binary encoding. For \(u\geq0\), let \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(b\) bits and no leading zeroes. Encode an integer \(a\) by a sign bit followed by \(\operatorname{code}(|a|)\), with 0 denoting a nonnegative integer and 1 a negative integer; negative zero is invalid. A complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(m)\operatorname{code}(r)\), followed for each \(j=1,\ldots,r\) by the signed code of \(a_j\) and \(\operatorname{code}(e_{j1}),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(e_{jm})\), with no trailing bits. Require \(m\geq1\). The machine halts and outputs NO on every malformed encoding.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program with a finite tape alphabet, ordinary discrete transitions and unbounded work tapes, without advice or an oracle. On every input it must halt after finitely many transitions; its running time need not satisfy a polynomial, elementary or other prescribed bound. Its program is independent of \(m,r\), all degrees and all coefficients. The input supplies only the polynomial, without additional height-comparison predicates or a promise of solvability. The question concerns decision of existence; a YES output need not itself contain a rational tuple.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify one effective algorithm and prove termination and exact correctness on every polynomial in the stated domain, together with rejection of invalid input. A negative answer must prove that no such total correct Turing machine exists. Recognizing only polynomials that have a rational zero, excluding polynomial-time algorithms, or proving undecidability for equations with integer-constrained unknowns or added predicates does not establish the required negation. Any conditional result must be identified as conditional and does not alone settle this unconditional question.
cards.status_note: Explicitly open over Q in the cited rational-solvability sources. A bounded primary-source check through 14 September 2026 located no resolution of this exact question. Checked recent results prove undecidability over rings of integers or after adjoining height-comparison predicates; neither settles existence of an unrestricted total rational-solvability decider. This is a formulation and source-scope audit, not an independent verification of every cited proof.

cards.title: Polynomial-time, polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
cards.formal: Does there exist a constant \(C>0\) and a classical randomized algorithm A running in polynomial time such that, for every rank-n rational lattice basis B, A outputs a nonzero integer vector z satisfying \(\Vert Bz\Vert _{2}\le n^{C} \lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L}(B))\) with probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: The input is an explicitly encoded matrix \(B\in \mathbb{Q} ^{d\times n}, d\ge n\ge 1\), with linearly independent columns. Each rational entry is given by a binary numerator and positive binary denominator. \(\mathrm{L}(B)=\{Bz:z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{n}\}\) is the lattice, and \(\lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L})=\min \{\Vert v\Vert _{2}:0\ne v\in \mathrm{L}\}\) is the length of a shortest nonzero vector in the Euclidean norm \(\Vert v\Vert _{2}=(\sum_{i}v_{i}^{2})^{1/2}\). Rank n, rather than ambient dimension d or coefficient magnitude, controls the approximation factor. There must be one polynomial P such that every run halts in at most \(\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{L})\) bit operations, where L is the input’s total bit length; output bits and random bits are counted. Randomness consists of independent fair bits. Require z to be a nonzero integer vector on every run, while the length guarantee may fail with probability at most \(1/3\). Both P and C are independent of all input parameters. There are no distributional, uniqueness, conditioning, ideal-lattice or basis-quality promises. A deterministic algorithm would also qualify. The one-dimensional case is exactly solvable by a basis vector. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No classical polynomial-time algorithm with any fixed polynomial approximation factor was found for unrestricted Euclidean search SVP. Recent termination guarantees count costly subroutine calls, and the August conditional hardness theorem concerns constant factors. The card explicitly allows bounded-error classical randomization.

cards.title: Capacity of the two-user Gaussian interference channel
cards.formal: Determine \(F(a,b,\mathrm{P}_{1},\mathrm{P}_{2},\lambda )=\sup _{(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(a,b,\mathrm{P}_{1},\mathrm{P}_{2})}[\lambda R_{1}+(1- \lambda )R_{2}]\) for every \(a,b\in \mathbb{R}\), finite \(\mathrm{P}_{1},\mathrm{P}_{2}\ge 0\) and \(\lambda \in [0,1]\). Here C is the capacity region of \(Y_{1},t=X_{1},t+aX_{2},t+Z_{1},t\) and \(Y_{2},t=bX_{1},t+X_{2},t+Z_{2},t\) with independent messages, average power constraints, no feedback or cooperation, and vanishing average decoding error, as defined below.
cards.definitions: For a block of n uses, messages \(M_{i}\) are independent and uniform on \(\{1,\ldots ,K_{i,n}\}\). Transmitter i applies a deterministic encoder \(f_{i,n}:\{1,\ldots ,K_{i,n}\}\to \mathbb{R} ^{n}\) depending only on its own message. Its codebook satisfies \((nK_{i,n})^{- 1}\sum _{m=1}^{K_{i,n}}\sum _{t=1}^{n} f_{i,n}(m)_{t}^{2}\le \mathrm{P}_{i}\). All \(Z_{i,t}\) are mutually independent \(N(0,1)\) random variables independent of the messages. Receiver i applies a measurable decoder \(g_{i,n}:\mathbb{R} ^{n}\to \{1,\ldots ,K_{i,n}\}\) to its own received vector. The probability that either decoded message is wrong is averaged over both messages and all noise. A nonnegative pair \((R_{1},R_{2})\) is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes with this error tending to zero and \(\liminf _{n\to \infty} n^{- 1} \log _{2} K_{i,n}\ge R_{i}\) for \(i=1,2\). C is the closure of achievable pairs, measured in bits per real channel use. Gains, powers and both codebooks are known to all terminals. Arbitrary encoding across time and predetermined time sharing with power allocation are permitted; transmitters have no messages in common, output feedback, or communication between them. C is compact, convex and downward closed, so the nonnegative supporting function F uniquely determines it.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function g on all real a,b, all finite real \(\mathrm{P}_{1},\mathrm{P}_{2}\ge 0\), and all real \(\lambda \in [0,1]\), and prove in Lean that |\(g- F(a,b,\mathrm{P}_{1},\mathrm{P}_{2},\lambda )|\le 1/100\) pointwise throughout that domain, in the units stated in the definitions. The answer must establish lower and upper bounds with this uniform error guarantee. An exact determination also qualifies. A finite set of sample values, an uncertified plot, or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit does not determine the curve. No predetermined formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed. This numerical acceptance criterion does not assert exact equality with a conjectured curve.

cards.title: Optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance tradeoff
cards.formal: Determine \(R_{2}(\delta )=\limsup _{n}\to \infty  (1/n)\log _{2} A_{2}(n,\lceil \delta n\rceil )\) for every fixed real \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\), where \(A_{2}(n,d)\) is the largest size of a binary length-n code with minimum Hamming distance at least d.
cards.definitions: A code C is any nonempty subset of \(\{0,1\}^{n}\); it need not be linear or efficiently encodable or decodable. The Hamming distance \(d_{H}(x,y)\) is the number of coordinates on which x and y differ. Require \(d_{H}(x,y)\ge d\) for every pair of distinct codewords \(x,y\in C; a\) singleton satisfies this condition vacuously. \(A_{2}(n,d)\) is the maximum of |C| over all such subsets. A code has rate \((\log _{2}|C|)/n\), measured in information bits per transmitted bit, and relative distance \(d/n\). The ceiling fixes integer rounding. The limsup permits code families on a subsequence of blocklengths; existence of a full limit is not assumed. \(\delta\) is fixed before n grows. All logarithms in this card are base two unless stated otherwise. The binary entropy function is \(h_{2}(t)=- t \log _{2}t- (1- t)\log _{2}(1- t)\), with \(0 \log _{2}0=0\). The endpoint regimes are known: \(R_{2}(0)=1\) and \(R_{2}(\delta )=0\) for \(1/2\le \delta \le 1\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function g on all real \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\), and prove in Lean that |\(g- R_{2}(\delta )|\le 1/100\) pointwise throughout that domain, in the units stated in the definitions. The answer must establish lower and upper bounds with this uniform error guarantee. An exact determination also qualifies. A finite set of sample values, an uncertified plot, or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit does not determine the curve. No predetermined formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed. This numerical acceptance criterion does not assert exact equality with a conjectured curve. For a lower bound \(\ell\)\((\delta )\), prove that for every \(\varepsilon >0\) arbitrarily large n admit codes of rate at least \(\ell\)\((\delta )- \varepsilon\) with distance at least \(\lceil \delta n\rceil\); for an upper bound \(u(\delta )\), prove that for every \(\varepsilon >0\) all sufficiently large n admit no such code of rate greater than \(u(\delta )+\varepsilon\). The proposed g must lie within \(1/100\) of the true rate throughout the domain, and polynomial-time construction or decoding is not required.

cards.title: Effective classification of polynomially testable hereditary graph properties
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm which, given a finite family F of finite simple graphs, decides whether induced-F-freeness admits a one-sided dense-model tester sampling at most \(C\cdot \varepsilon ^{- c}\) vertices, for some constants C,c depending only on F?
cards.definitions: The input to the classification algorithm is a finite list of adjacency matrices; the empty list is allowed. Let \(\mathrm{P}_{F}\) contain exactly the finite simple graphs with no induced subgraph isomorphic to any member of F. For an n-vertex graph G, define \(\operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P}_{F})\) as the minimum number of edge additions or deletions needed to obtain a graph in \(\mathrm{P}_{F}\) on the same vertex set, divided by \(n^{2}\); define the distance as +∞ when no such graph exists. For an integer s, the canonical tester chooses a uniformly random subset S of \(\min \{n,s\}\) distinct vertices, queries all adjacencies in S, and rejects exactly when \(G[S]\) contains an induced member of F. Say that F is polynomially testable if there are integers \(C,c\ge 1\) such that for every rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), every \(n\ge 1\) and every G with \(\operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P}_{F})>\varepsilon\), this tester with \(s=\lceil C\varepsilon ^{- c}\rceil\) rejects with probability at least \(2/3\). It automatically accepts every graph in \(\mathrm{P}_{F}\). The requested deterministic classification algorithm must halt on every finite F and answer YES exactly for these families. No runtime bound on that classification algorithm is imposed, and it need not output the constants C,c. Graph order n and accuracy \(\varepsilon\) are universally quantified in the property being classified; they are not additional inputs to the classification algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

cards.title: Polynomial testability versus distance estimation
cards.formal: For every isomorphism-invariant property P of finite simple graphs with \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) nonempty for every \(n\ge 1\), does existence of a uniform randomized tester using polynomially many queries in \(1/\varepsilon\), independently of n, imply existence of such an additive-\(\varepsilon\) distance estimator, in the dense model defined below?
cards.definitions: \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) is a nonempty subset of graphs on \([n]\), invariant under vertex permutations. For \(n\ge 2, \operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P})=\min _{H\in \mathrm{P}_{n}}|E(G)\triangle E(H)|/\operatorname{binom}(n,2)\); for \(n=1\) it is zero. An algorithm receives n and an integer \(t\ge 2\), with \(\varepsilon =1/t\), and accesses G only by adaptive queries asking whether a specified unordered pair is an edge. A tester returns a bit, accepts each \(G\in \mathrm{P}_{n}\) with probability \(\ge 2/3\) and rejects each G with \(\operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P})\ge \varepsilon\) with probability \(\ge 2/3\); no condition is imposed between those cases. Polynomial testability means there exist one probabilistic Turing oracle machine and constants \(C,a\ge 1\) with at most \(Ct^{a}\) adjacency queries on every input and every execution. An estimator is another such uniform machine and constants \(C' ,b\ge 1\), using at most \(C' t^{b}\) queries and returning a binary-encoded rational q with \(\Pr [|q- \operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P})|\le 1/t]\ge 2/3\) for every G. Computation between queries and total output length have no prescribed bound, but every execution terminates. Coins are independent fair bits; programs and constants may depend on P and cannot depend on n,t or G. Neither algorithm receives a description of P or graph-dependent advice. This asks only the polynomial-testability implication named in the title. The stronger quantitative \(q_{\mathrm{P}}(\operatorname{poly}(\varepsilon ))\) conversion in source Problem 5.4 is not asserted equivalent to it.

cards.title: Private PAC sample complexity from VC and Littlestone dimensions
cards.formal: Is there a universal polynomial p such that every nonempty finite Boolean concept class C on a finite nonempty domain X admits a realizable, possibly improper PAC learner using some number $m\le p(1+\mathrm{VC}(C),1+\log^*\mathrm{LD}(C))$ of independent labeled examples, with error at most \(1/10\) and confidence at least \(9/10\), while satisfying $(1,1/(100m^2))$-differential privacy? The learning guarantee must hold for every distribution on the domain and every target concept in C. Computation time is unrestricted. Take both dimensions to be at least one; constant classes can be handled separately.
cards.definitions: A concept class is a finite set of functions from a domain X to \(\{0,1\}\). \(\operatorname{VC}(C)\) is the largest size of a subset of X on which all binary labelings occur. \(LD(C)\) is the greatest depth of a complete binary tree labeled by domain points such that every root-to-leaf edge-label sequence is realized by a concept. The function log-star counts base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. A learner may output a hypothesis outside C. Privacy requires $\Pr[A(S)\in E]\le e\Pr[A(S\prime)\in E]+1/(100m^2)$ whenever the two m-record samples differ by replacement of one record. Here X is finite, distributions on X are arbitrary probability vectors, and a learner is a probability kernel from length-m labeled samples to the finite set \(\{0,1\}^{X}\) of hypotheses. The sample size m is a positive integer chosen for C before the target and distribution. For every target \(h\in C\) and distribution D on X, with probability at least \(9/10\) over m independent draws \(x_{i}\) from D and learner randomness, the returned hypothesis has D-probability of disagreement with h at most \(1/10\). Privacy holds for all labeled samples, including unrealizable ones, and all subsets E of the hypothesis set. The same kernel and m work for all D,h. This finite-domain convention retains the finite-class target: points in an arbitrary domain with the same label vector \((h(x))_{h\in C}\) can be identified, giving at most \(2^{|}C|\) cells and preserving both dimensions. A learner on those cells lifts to the original domain. No running-time or computable-representation requirement is imposed.

cards.title: Optimal error for pure-DP continual counting
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as \(T\to \infty , E(T)=\inf _{M} \max _{x\in \{0,1\}^{T}} E_{Y\sim M_{x}}[\max _{1\le t\le T}|Y_{t}- \sum_{i=1}^{t} x_{i}|]\), where the infimum is over all causal \((1/2,0)\)-differentially private mechanisms defined below.
cards.definitions: For an integer \(T\ge 2, a\) mechanism is a family of Borel probability distributions \(M_{x}\) on \(\mathbb{R} ^{T}\), one for each binary stream \(x\in \{0,1\}^{T}\). Its output \(Y_{t}\) is released immediately after observing \(x_{t}\). Causality means that whenever x and \(x'\) have the same first t bits, the marginal distributions of \((Y_{1},\ldots ,Y_{t})\) under \(M_{x}\) and \(M_{x}'\) are equal. The horizon T is known before the first output. Streams are fixed inputs, not adaptively chosen in response to outputs. Neighbors differ in exactly one bit, and pure privacy requires \(M_{x}(S)\le \exp (1/2)M_{x}' (S)\) for every pair of neighbors and every Borel \(S\subseteq \mathbb{R} ^{T}\). This protects the entire joint transcript, with no additive failure allowance. There is no restriction on computation, memory, real precision, output integrality or monotonicity; internal randomness may be correlated across times. A different family of probability distributions may be chosen for each T. The maximum over streams is outside the expectation; the maximum over time is inside it. The infimum is used without assuming attainment. \(E(T)\) is finite, for example because a data-independent all-zero transcript has error at most T. All logarithms in asymptotic comparisons may use any fixed base greater than one.
cards.answer_criterion: Determine an asymptotic rate \(g(T)\) and prove constants \(c,C>0\) and \(T_{0}\) such that \(c g(T)\le E(T)\le C g(T)\) for every \(T\ge T_{0}\). The upper guarantee must be achievable by permitted causal pure-private mechanisms, and the lower guarantee must cover all such mechanisms. Constants may not depend on T. The expected maximum absolute-error criterion must be the same on both sides.
